I have the honour to inform the House that I have received the following letter :
Ottawa, July 9, 1903.
Sir,-I have the honour to inform you that His Excellency the Governor General will proceed to the Senate Chamber on Friday the tenth instant at five o'clock p.m., for the purpose of giving assent to certain Bills which have passed the Senate and House of Commons during the present session.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,
F. S. MAUDE, Major, Governor General's Secretary.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 220) respecting the Government Post Office Savings Bank. He said : This is the Bill of which I made mention , some time ago. It is composed of a single clause, and provides that there shall be a reserve of 10 per cent in gold or guaranteed debentures on the amount of the deposits in the government savings banks.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries if that correspondence has yet been brought down which was asked for some two months ago, and which has been promised to me on several occasions ?
I really thought it was on the Table of the House, because I signed the papers about six days ago. I will see about it.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I wish to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of the Interior to a statement which was made in the North-west Legislative Assembly some days ago by the Premier in respect to what are known as the Barr colonists. In view of the very large immigration which is taking place into this country, I think it is of the very highest importance that when serious statements are made respecting mismanagement and the non-fulfilment of pledges on the part of those who promote large immigration schemes, it is the duty of the government to make an exhaustive examination into them. Especially is this the case in the matter to which I desire to draw the attention of the hon. minister, because, if my information is correct, the statement which was made is a very serious one, and it was made by a gentleman who is well and favourably known throughout the country, a gentleman who has had a good deal of parliamentary experience, and who, I am sure, in making the statement, has kept well within the mark. The Barr colony is one of the first large bodies of English immigrants who have been induced to come and settle in the North-west Territories. That class of immigration is a most desirable class, and it would be a great misfortune indeed if, because of incorrect or untruthful statements or unfulfilled promises, the hopes of the immigraijts were not to be realized. It is a notorious fact that many statements have been made in Canadian, as well as in British, newspapers, by those who profess to be of the Barr colony, expressive of their dissatisfaction with the treatment which they have received. I think statements of that kind ought to be discounted to some extent ; but when a responsible gentleman like the Premier of the North-west Territories makes such a statement as 1 propose to present to the House, I think it is the bounden duty of the government to make an exhaustive examination into it, and to lay the facts before

tlie people as quickly as possible. I will not take up the time of the House, but X will merely read the statement which has been handed to me, and which is taken from the Regina 'Leader' of July 2nd. The matter was evidently being discussed in the territorial legislature, and this is the report of Mr. Haultain's remarks in closing the discussion :
Mr. Haultain closed the debate in a few words. Referring to Mr. Clinkskill's speech with reference to Mr. Barr, the premier said he did not wish to use his position in the House to make charges against Mr. Barr when the gentleman could not be present to reply. At the same time, he thought some remarks on the subject ought to be made, and had very properly been made. From conversation he had had with members of the colony on the trail between Saskatoon and Battleford, he was convinced there had been some gross mismanageemnt in connection with the colony, and something worse than gross mismanagement in certain financial dealings with it. The Dominion government by allowing Mr. Barr to reserve a certain number of townships had to that extent recognized the scheme, and it was the duty of that government to have all the charges cleared up by a thorough investigation. He said this was in the interests of the territories, and in the interests of some of the best immigrants that ever came into the country.
If this is a correct report of the statement made by Mr. Haultain, I think there cannot be two opinions as to the advisability of having some person make an exhaustive examination into the charges alleged. I think it is due to Mr. Barr, who is at the head of the colony ; it is due to the government, who set aside certain townships for the use of the colonists ; and it is due to the country, because if the allegations which are made are not disposed of satisfactorily, they will prevent that tide of immigration coming from the old country which we all sincerely desire. I wish to ascertain from the hon. Minister of the Interior what has been done, or what he intends to do, to clear this matter up. He is aware, of course, of the statements which have been made in the papers in the old country by members of the Barr colony expressing their dissatisfaction with some of the arrangements made.

Mr. Speaker, the statement which was made by Mr. Haultain in the North-w'est assembly, and to which my hon. friend has called attention, has not been brought to my attention before to-day. The relations between the department and Mr. Barr of the Barr colony, are extremely simple. Mr. Barr conceived a scheme of inducing a large number of people to settle in the North-west. He represented to the department that there would be difficulty in carrying out the scheme unless the department agreed that it would hold available for homestead entry by the persons whom he would select a certain amount of land for a certain number of Mr. CLARKE.
months. That has been done in some other cases for some other people, generally with results that were not unsatisfactory, although at present, owing to the largely increased influx of settlers, it is a practice which the department may not be able to follow in the future. There did not seem, however, to be any difficulty in making this arrangement with Mr. Barr, but the only arrangement which the department had with that gentleman was that it would hold a certain amount of land a certain length of time, for the purpose of granting applications for homestead entries within that tract to those whose names Mr. Barr would furnish, subject to the reservation that the applications should be on bebalf of bona fide persons desiring to settle. That arrangement was continued at the instance of the Deputy Minister of the Interior who was in England. The department saw difficulties in carrying the scheme into effect, but the House will understand that in matters relating to immigration, where you have to deal with human beings, who think they know best, and are not always willing to accept advice, we very often have to do what we ourselves would not have suggested in order to avoid losing a considerable amount of immigration. In this case we would have preferred that these settlers had come to our officers in London and put themselves in their hands. Had they done this, they would have been handled better and with less trouble and there would have been no dissatisfaction. They, however, would not do that. The Deputy Minister of the Interior was in London at the time, and after considerable correspondence by cable, he advised that it would be better in the long run to give way to their proposition, because if we had refused, we would, in all probability, have been advertised as discouraging settlement, and this would have had an injurious influence on intending emigrants. As I felt considerable doubt of the ability of Mr. Barr to handle these people, I gave Instructions to the officers of my department to make precisely the same preparations to handle tiiis colony as if Mr. Barr had nothing to do with it. The people who undertook to handle that colony were not sufficiently experienced, they did not know what had to be done in the North-west on the arrival of a large party of that kind, and I instructed the officers of my department to take the same steps as if these people were depending on the government officials solely to look after them. My officers did so, but of course they could not interfere until the colonists made up their minds to abandon Mr. Barr. Our officers stood aside until called in, and then they did whatever was necessary. I have not had before me any complaints whatever regarding the nature of the services granted by the officers of my department. On the contrary, I think it was generally admitted that they showed zeal

and efficiency, and under all the circumstances were very successful. Tents were planted at regular distances and every attempt made to prevent unnecessary suffering, but of course one could easily understand that, in the case of a large number of people coming from England, who had previously no experience of hardship of any kind, they would necessarily have to go through what they would 'consider hardships, hut what the average Canadian or what members of this House would endure cheerfully tuid not think twice about it. So far as financial relations are concerned, there were none between Mr. Barr and the department. Our arrangement simply consisted in the fact that we held a certain quantity Of land for a certain length of time at the disposal of these colonists. We have no knowledge whatever of any financial relations which did exist between them and Mr. Barr. They made their own arrangements with Mr. Barr, in London, England. Any of them who took the trouble to consult the officers of my department in London were told that there was no necessity to employ Mr. Barr or anybody else, but that they could make their applications directly without charge, except the ordinary government fee, so that the financial arrangements, if any, between the members of the colony and Mr. Barr were voluntary arrangements made in London, without the co-operation of the officers of the government of their knowledge as regards details. We know at present nothing whatever about Mr. Barr's financial arrangements except that it has transpired, in the course of correspondence, that he received a commission from the steamship companies. lion, members will, therefore, see that there is nothing before the department to justify any investigation at present. It is somewhat difficult to see how an investigation can he held into the financial arrangements made in London, England, by this colony with Mr. Barr, especially in the absence of Mr. Barr, who, I understand, is not now in the colony.
speakername: The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton).

speechtext: He is in Winnipeg.

It would be difficult, under the circumstances, to make a satisfactory investigation. I quite recognize what my hon. friend says that if there are distinct allegations of impropriety in connection with the financial relations between the members of the colony and Mr. Barr himself, it would be well that these should be cleared up as fully as possible, but whether the facts which can be brought before us will be sufficient to justify our going into an inquiry, I could not say at the moment. I will undertake to procure the debate, if it is reported, to which my hon. friend referred, and endeavour to find out upon what specific facts and allegations, any charges of impropriety are based, and then determine whether I can properly go on with an investigation
or not. Possibly I may have that information before my estimates are through.

This matter is one of more than ordinary importance because it involves very largely the question as to what kind of immigration we shall have in the future. It was announced that this settlement of Barr colonists was the most satisfactory scheme of immigration which we had up to that time, and that they were the best class of colonists who had ever come into Canada. I do not think that time has led us to change our opinion in that regard, but just in proportion as they were a superior class of immigrants, the attention of the public, both here and at home, was directed to this scheme. And it is all important that, whatever we may do, we shall make it clear to the people of Great Britain that the representations made to immigrants in Canada will be substantially carried out, that whatever prospects are held forth to people coming to settle in our great west will, in the main, be realized. Now, this matter, of course, might have taken the position of being quite unconnected with the government. But, as Mr. Haultain points out, it does appear that the government was to some extent connected with it. And it further appears, by the statement of the Minister of the Interior, that that was the fact. Mr. Haultain says that the Dominion government, by allowing Mr. Barr to reserve a certain number of townships, to that extent recognized the scheme ; and so it was the duty of the government to have all the charges cleared up by a thorough investigation. I understood the Minister of the Interior to say- though I am sorry to say, I cannot at all times hear at this distance what is said- that probably he would determine upon an investigation. I understood him to say also that there were difficulties in the way of investigation. It will appear perfectly clear, I think, from this statement of the'minister, that, although the department did not get complete control of that colonization scheme, it was so far connected with it as that it must be held to a large extent responsible for the success of the scheme. And, whether they are held in the strict sense responsible, whether it would be fair for the people or the members of this House to hold that government strictly to account in this matter, I think the hon. minister in control of the department will recognize, as a matter of public interest, as a matter affecting the settlement of the west, that in the future it is essential that the government and the department should take such active measures as will make it clear that whenever immigrants come from any land, particularly when a superior class of immigrants come from Great Britain, if there is an error at all, it shall be an error on the side of pay-

I suppose that what is said by the Minister of the Interior that he has no precise knowledge of the relations between Mr. Barr and the colonists, and particularly of their financial arrangement, must be accepted as a very strong reason why there is not ground at this moment for an investigation. At the present time the matter of immigration is of such great importance, perhaps the most important matter we have engaging our attention, that it will excuse a certain amount of solicitude on the part of the members of this House in seeing that nothing whatever should be done to prejudice what is by far i the most desirable class of immigrants we

could hope to receive in this country. Of course, the House, perhaps, knows even less than the Minister of the Interior as to the financial arrangements made between Mr. Barr and the persons whom he induced to come to this country. But from statements I have seen in the press, I would infer that there must have been something unsatisfactory in the financial arrangements made by Mr. Barr with them ; for if I am not mistaken, I have seen it recently stated that Mr. Barr, in arriving at a settlement with these colonists at Saskatoon, or some point in that neighbourhood, had refunded to them, or to some of them, certain sums of money which he had no doubt received from them. Now if that be the case, there must have been some ground for dissatisfaction on the part of these immigrants, as apparently their reasoning prevailed so far with Mr. Barr, the promoter of this movement, that he found it expedient to refund certain moneys that he had received at their hands. That being the case, it seems to me the government, or the department over which the hon. gentleman presides, should at once make it their business to ascertain as quickly and as completely as possible if there was anything improper in the relations which existed between this gentleman and the immigrants whom he induced to come to this country. The great care that is being taken by the government, and in which they are supported, I think, by every one wishing well to Canada, and hoping to see the growth of Canada made as rapid as possible in the future, would show how exceedingly important it is that we should do nothing whatever to prejudice any one of British birth or nationality, who may be looking forward to leaving his home, against coming to Canada. Now the proportion which we are to-day receiving of British immigrants is very satisfactory, we are apparently gaining at a very rapid rate in the proportion in which our immigrants of British origin bear to immigrants who are at this time going into the United States, and, of course, the United States is our great rival for that class of immigration which we consider so very desirable.
There is one thing which apparently the British immigrant, when he goes abroad, is exceedingly prompt to take advantage of, and that is the columns of the British press. In the mother country we find that journals of the very highest class, the London 'Times' and other first-class journals, seem to look upon it as a duty to open their columns to anything whatever in the nature of a complaint that may be offered by any British subject who has recently gone abroad. It would seem to be quite characteristic of these British immigrants to resort very promptly to this means of ventilating any grievance, either real or imaginary, which they conceive to exist. The consequence is of course, that, having this habit of appealing to their fellow citizeus at home through the press, and through the most respectable journals of that country, one or two dissatisfied immigrants coming into Canada are capable of doing an enormous amount of harm in prejudicing the people of the British islands against Canada ; they are capable of doing an enormous amount to nullify the great and proper efforts being made by the Department of the Interior, for the government of Canada, to secure the confidence of the British people and to turn the feet of intending immigrants in this direction. I think we ought to pay the greatest possible attention to anything that may even unwarrantably excite suspicion or dissatisfaction in the minds of immigrants. The Minister of the Interior has very properly, to my mind, observed that difficulties or comparative hardships that may be looked upon by our own people as trifling matters of every day occurrence, might be regarded by people coming from the old country, and by a class which perhaps never had occasion to rough it, as great hardships. No doubt a short acquaintance with Canada and a short experience in our western country has already taught these people to look with comparative indifference upon circumstances and upon features of apparent hardship which perhaps to them at first seemed very disagreeable indeed. The main point is this, that while receiving their first and early impressions at a time when they have not acquired such experience as would enable them to judge carefully and to speak impartially, they are prompt to speak without waiting to acquire that experience or that maturity of judgment ; they become so dissatisfied that they are at once placed in a position in which they become capable of exciting a strong feeling of dissatisfaction and suspicion on the part of the great mass of people in the mother country who, we have reason to believe from time to time, are thinking about changing their homes and coming to this country.
Now it would seem to me that, with the very large and well organized machinery which the government has instituted in the mother country for the purpose of reaching the ears of intending immigrants, a machinery which covers to a large extent the whole of the British islands, there is no reason why any gentleman should be allowed to take a position in connection with immigrants to this country which Mr. Barr seems to have taken. I would imagine that the middle man, the organizer of such an expedition, is entirely unnecessary at this moment in handling the immigrants who are looking towards Canada. In fact it would appear from what has transpired in connection with the Barr colony that there is a great and real danger that the interference of such a person is misehievi-ous, and that the immigrants would be in

better bands if they continued to place their confidence in, and to receive their advice from, the officers of the department. For that reneon I think it would require great caution on the part of the government before they entered into any arrangement whatever with Mi\ Barr, or any other gentleman who undertook to do what lie seems to have done in this case, in the direction of assigning to him any portion of the homestead lands of our country, as in this case was done by setting apart certain townships. It would appear from the whole history of this expedition that whatever purpose might have been intended by setting apart these townships so as to keep the Barr colonists together, and to form an all British settlement, it was to a very serious extent at least defeated by the result of the experience of these colonists. If I am not mistaken, a very large portion of the party which set out for Canada under Mr. Barr's leadership, did not eventually settle down in that part of the Dominion which was assigned to them by the Department of the Interior. I understand that only a comparatively limited portion of the party finally took up the lands in the townships which had been allotted to them. If I am not mistaken, I think quite a considerable portion of them found themselves quite as well suited and made settlements at some points some hundreds of miles on this side of that portion of the Dominion which had been set apart for their use.
There is another point in connection with the Barr colonists that seems to be of very great importance and that is the fact that quite a considerable number of these immigrants, instead of proceeding to the lands which were set apart for them and homesteading there, adopted what I think is the much wiser course of going into the employment of farmers already settled in Canada whereby they would have the advantage of acquiring a knowledge of the ways of the country and of acquiring that experience without which no man in the west can hope to be a successful farmer. It seems to me that instead of locating lands in certain portions of the country upon which large bodies of immigrants might settle down in compact bodies of all British settlements it would he much more important and) more likely to conduce to the advantage both of the immigrants and of the country if the opposite course were followed and if an effort were made, instead of placing these men in compact settlements, to scatter them about as much as possible among older settlers who have acquired an experience of Canadian conditions and have learned how to make a success of farming in this country. That process of settlement which seems much more desirable than the one adopted by Mr. Barr is one which would entirely exclude gentlemen like Mr. Barr from this work of colonization. It would be a work which would be more Mr. BELL.
properly done through the Department of the Interior. That department, with all its machinery and with its officials in the mother country and in Canada, could deal with the immigrant individually when he came to this country and it could place him upon a farm where he would have the advantage of Canadian neighbours with a large acquaintance of Canadian conditions, and'better still, it might, if possible, induce him to accept employment with a farmer in this country as a hired man and thus enable him to acquire a knowledge of Canadian conditions which would practically guarantee success when the time came that he could take up his work as a farmer in Canada. The fact which I mentioned in my first remarks tfiat representations had been made that Mr. Barr has refunded certain sums of money to the members of his party would seem to show- that there ivas really something in the contract or arrangement made between Mr. Barr and the colonists which was faulty and it is unfortunate that this was accomplished by Mr. Barr in consequence of the standing and position he secured with the department, which so far endorsed his scheme as to set apart and put into the hands of this gentleman a large amount of Canadian territory for the exclusive use of his party. There cau be no doubt that a gentleman, when he went to a party of intending immigrants, would have a better chance of procuring their consent to his proposal if he went with the endorsa-tion of tiie Department of the Interior and of the Canadian government, and were in a position to say :	I have so far acquired
the endorsation of the Canadian government that they have seen fit to interfere with the ordinary course of their methods in settling the lands of Canada by assigning to me certain townships in tlie western portion of the country. It does seem to me to be of the last necessity that the government should never in any case at all set its seal upon arrangements of this character, which, as the lion. Minister of the Interior has very properly observed, are to the last degree unnecessary. There is no occasion for a gentleman like Mr. Barr, with his very limited knowledge of our country, to go into this transaction with the impression that he can better organize a party and better conduct it to homes in the west than the officials of the Dominion government. The facts of this case would seem to argue that the interference of persons of this character is to say the least of it mischievous and that the government, instead of encouraging anything of that kind, would rather be serving the interests of the country if it would discredit the efforts of gentlemen like Mr. Barr, and confine the work of immigration largely to the officials of the department to work with their sanction and consent and for whose actions the government would be held responsible to the people, to this House and to the immigrants themselves. The

whole circumstances would seem to apply the necessity that the government should as soon as possible acquire absolute knowledge of this transaction. There may be very little ground whatever for the statements that are being made, but the fact that they are being made and circulated in the mother country is an important fact, because it is interfering with the success of our immigration system, a system upon which the people of Canada are spending a large amount of money and a system to which they look with a great deal of confidence to fill up Canada with a British population. I do not think I need say anything more beyond this that these irregular immigration agents like Mr. Barr should be discouraged and that everything done with the consent of the department should be done by the officials of the department so that the control of the movement will be in the hands of the government and the government will be responsible for any miscarriage or bad result.
Will my hon. friend send me the interview; I have not seen it.

I will give it to the hon. minister as soon as I have concluded. That statement purports to emanate from Mr. Preston and as published in the Westminster ' Gazette ' it seems to Indicate that Mr. Barr in the first place made all his arrangements with the Canadian government and then went over to start liis propaganda for the purpose of Inducing this immigration movement; And, that Mr. Barr from the first was practically indicated by the Canadian government as a special immigration agent for the purpose of bringing these people to western Canada. I do not know whether that is a fact or not-of course I do not know if Mr. Preston made use of these words, but that is the statement of the case as presented to the representative of the Westminster ' Gazette ' if the words of that representative are to be believed; and that is the statement that appears in the Canadian ' Gazette ' of the 28th of May. I would have thought that under these circumstances it would have been the duty of the government to make the fullest possible enquiry into the character, capacity, and ability of Mr. Barr before lending himself to a movement of that kind and before allowing him to superintend such a large immigration as that of 2,000 people from the British Isles. I do not know whether or not the Minister of the Interior or his officers made any such investigation or inquiry, and I do not want to do Mr. Barr any Injustice because he is not here to answer for himself; 'but we know that there have been reports repeatedly circulated through the press of this country which would seem to indicate that the government In giving to Mr. Barr the control of this expedition had not made a careful

investigation into his record or into his cnnacity to conduct a large movement of this kind. Then the interview proceeds with something that seems to me to be very much more significant than what I have read. Mr. Preston continues as follows :-
Arrangements were made with the Elder-Dempster Line, by which Mr. Barr was to receive a commission on the bookings of his party, just in the same way as any other booking office would have acted towards any emigration agent. Under this arrangement he will probably receive 25s. per emigrant. He made no secret whatever to the Canadian government that he was to be remunerated in this way. In granting this concession to Mr. Barr, our government had no intention to divest itself of any responsibility in connection with the constituent elements of the party. It was specially laid down that they were all going out to engage in agricultural pursuits. In point of fact the emigrants paid their entrance fees for their homesteads through myself.
The statement is made here, that under an arrangement with the Elder Dempster line to which the Canadian government was a consenting party, Mr. Barr was to receive a commission of twenty-five shillings per immigrant. I can hardly believe myself that any such arrangement could have been made or that the Canadian government was a consenting party to it.

There is nothing at all to indicate that the Canadian government had anything to do with the payment of a commission by the Elder Dempster Company; we had absolutely nothing to do with it. When I was making my statement I said that we were informed that the commission had been paid.

It does not say by whom the arrangement was made and it is quite open to what the minister suggests; that in the first place it was entirely an arrangement between Mr. Barr and the steamship company, although that is not perfectly plain from the words. However, under some arrangement made by some person, he was to receive twenty-five shillings per head from the Elder Dempster line, and the significant part of it is that he made no secret to the Canadian government that he was to be remunerated in this way. It seems to have been part of the arrangement made in London (when Mr. Barr went forward for the purpose of conducting this propaganda as it is called), that Mr. Barr was to receive a commission of twenty-five shillings per head upon each of these immigrants, amounting to the sum- if there were 2,000 of them-of about $12,000; that he made no secret of this to the Canadian government, and that the Canadian government were fully aware of it. If Mr. Preston's statements are correctly reported and if they are to be believed, it does seem to me that the relations between the Canadian government and Mr. Barr were not quite of that simple character
Mr. BORDEN fHalifax).
which the Minister of the Interior would seek to impress upon the House to-day. Further on Mr. Preston delivers himself as follows :

Mr. Speaker, I concur in every word that has fallen from the lips of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Borden). Wisely or unwisely, truthfully or untruthfully, the people of Canada and the people of England, believe that Mr. Barr, was the agent of the government of Canada. That is the crucial point in this matter. Very often people get an erroneous idea ; but when once that idea is entertained by the people, it must be removed from their minds before the conclusion which they have reached will lie erased. I am persuaded that the public impression is pretty widespread, not only in Canada but in England, and in all countries from which we expect immigration, that the government of Canada has had an unworthy agreement of some kind with Mr. Barr. If that is not true-and I hope for the sake of the government of Canada and the people of Canada that it is not true-then no people should be more interested than the government of Canada, no man should be more 200
interested than the Minister of the Interior, in having the matter thoroughly and completely investigated, in order that there may be no shade of doubt in any man's mind that the government of Canada have acted honestly and honourably by the men it has invited to become citizens of this country. I was pained yesterday to read that Mr. Barr had been publicly pelted with rotten eggs in a most disgraceful way at the town of Regina, by the populace, or by a number of people, who claimed that they had been wronged by him. I say that is pelting the government of Canada. The pelting of Mr. Barr, in the eyes of the public of Europe, will be the pelting of the kon. Minister of the Interior. I would be very sorry to have a personal insult of that kind offered to any man in the cabinet, because it is an insult offered to me as a citizen of this country. I want the government to be, like Caesar's wife, above suspicion. It is an awful assumption to make, but we are bound constitutionally to make assumptions of a very sweeping character sometimes. I desire to read a few words which were uttered lately by Mr. Haultain in another place ; and we know that Mr. Haultain is not a partisan. I do not know particularly what politics he has. He seems to be a North-west man ; and we know that the gentlemen from the Nortk-ivest who are in this House, are ahead of the public in many instances, which is perhaps a very good thing to say of any men. Mr. Haultain is a North-west man ; and, occupying the responsible position he does, he is charged with maintaining the character and reputation of that country, and with looking after its interests; and he can do that in no better ivay than In seeing that every immigrant that comes to settle in the North-west is treated in an honest and honourable manner by the government of Canada. I want to see millions of people come and settle in this country, and I want to know that when they do come, they will send out favourable accounts: of the country in the" letters which tliejr write to their friends. These will influence immigration, more than anything, the hon. minister can do, because they wTill reflect the settler's impressions of the country, its government, its laws, and its administration of justice. According to the tales that are going around, Mr. Barr is looked upon as the representative of this government, and his conduct will reflect on the fair fame and integrity of Canada. Therefore, the Minister of the Interior should be the first person to feel sensitive on this point. The government's attempt to treat this matter liglitly will not be borne. The people will not permit their honour to be sullied at any time, especially when they are spending large sums of money for immigration purposes. The expenditure of that money is probably one of the best investments Canada can make; but charge that expenditure



witl>
the slightest taint, and for every dollar spent, $25 will not recompense the country for the injury it will do. Therefore when Mr. Haultaiu, the premier of the North-west, in whose country these immigrants will settle, charges this government, with, in some way, creating this impression on the minds of the immigrants, I care not how improperly it was created, that Mr. Barr was acting as their agent, it is their duty to clear the matter up. That impression exists, and the hon. gentleman can see that it exists, if he reads the papers of yesterday. The people of this country are a quiet pimple, not accustomed to be boisterous, but accustomed to wait for the vindication of justice in the courts on all occasions ; but I venture to say that if this government does not look out for itself, manifestations will take place all over the country, similar to that which took place at Regina ; because when the people do not get justice and) fair play, there is sufficient sense of right in the British bosom to cause them to resist violations of the constitution and to resort to rotten eggs, as was done at Regina yesterday.
Hear, hear.

I am glad that the lion. Postmaster General is aroused on this matter, and I apprehend that when he says ' hear, hear,' he realizes that a great wrong lias been done by the government of which he is a member, and is determined on behalf of the great province of Ontario to see that it is remedied.
The Minister of Labour 7

Y'es, and there are a number of excellent labourers in my county who tell me, that this minister, does not righteously represent the interests of labour in this country. Mr. Haultain says that the Dominion government, by allowing Mr. Barr to reserve a certain number of townships had to that extent recognized the scheme. I ask the minister, did the government allow Mr. Barr to reserve certain townships in the vicinity of those which were allotted to immigrants who "were coming to this country ? If he did, he did that which was a gross wrong. He enabled Mr. Barr to bring a number of settlers here, who would give value to the land reserved by him. and in that manner, a bargain was entered into, which wes most unjust to the people. No private individual should be allowed to make one dollar out of an immigration scheme. Better vote twice the money we do, if necessary, to encourage immigration, but be careful to preserve the poor immigrants from the machinations or the boodler. Let us keep these poor people out of the toils of the boodlers and speculators and grafters.

Does the hon. member interpret Mr. Haultain's statement to mean Mr. GOURLEY.
that Mr. Haultain believed Mr. Barr was to be permitted to make money out of the reserving of land for the colonists ?

Mr. Haultain used very guarded language. I shall read it to the hon. gentleman, and he may draw his own conclusion as I am drawing mine. Mr. Haultain said :
He did not wish to use his position in the House to make charges against Mr. Barr when that gentleman could not be present to reply. At the same time he thought that some remarks on the subject ought to he made and had very properly been made. Prom conversations he had had with members of the colony on the train, between Saskatchewan and Battleford, he was convinced that there had been some gross mismanagement in connection with the colony, and something worse than gross mismanagement in certain financial dealings with it.
My bon. friend may draw liis own conclusions. Mr. Haultain went on to add :
The Dominion government, by allowing Mr. Barr to reserve a certain number of townships for them, had to that extent recognized the scheme, and it was the duty of that government to have all the charges cleared up by a thorough investigation.
The hon. the Minister of the Interior may consider himself innocent, but what do the people think of the matter ? What do the people of England, Scotland, Ireland, Germany and Austria think of it 7 It is the public opinion of those countries with which we have to deal. The hon. minister may treat this matter with a smile, but how do the relatives of the people who came here consider it ? When these colonists write home and say that they have been defrauded by the government of this country, and by Mr. Barr, what will these people think ? I do not wish to make any sweeping charges against anybody, but Mr. Barr was recognized in Europe as tlie agent of the government. He occupied perhaps a stronger position as the agent of the government than Mr. Preston. Mr. Preston is the acknowledged agent of the government in England, and if he should do anything, that could be charged against him, this government would be compelled at once to have an investigation. Well, I undertake to say that this reverend clergyman, occupied in the minds of the people of England a stronger position, as an agent of this country, than even Mr. Preston. Everybody knows in what esteem these clergymen are held in England. England owes its vast domains in Africa and Asia largely to the missionary. It owes its influence largely to these men from Oxford and Cambridge, who are the possessors of fortunes, and who use their money, not for their personal benefit, but in promoting settlement In those countries. South Africa was largely brought under the flag of England by Mr. McKenzie, one of the most accomplished clergymen who ever left the old country ; and I have no doubt that the

people of England regarded Mr. Barr as a high minded, wealthy gentleman, who, in the interests of the empire, without any low desire of making money for himself, was bringing out colonists to settle in this, the empire's principal colony. They never dreamed that he was other than a philanthropist, a religious enthusiast, who desired to help this empire and its people and was spending his own fortune to promote the welfare of Canada and the empire.
Mr. Preston's interview would disabuse the minds of the English people of that mistaken impression.

I will undertake to say, knowing the history of England, knowing what has been done by English clergymen, as imperialists, In the work of settling the empire, that the very instant Mr. Barr appeared in any part of England, he would be regarded as one of the missionary priests who were devoting their energies to spreading the influence of the empire wherever they could. Hundreds of the clergymen of England, are doing this, every day, to their honour be it said, and Mr. Barr is the only clergyman of the Church of England I have ever heard of, who has prostituted his position for the purpose of making money out of the poor people. I believe that association has corrupted this gentleman, who might otherwise have been an honourable man. Possibly his contact with the government of Canada, in some way brought him from the high level of a clergyman of the Church of England down to the low level of a Canadian boodler. I ask you, Mr. Chairman
Address the Chair as Mr. Speaker.

My hon. friend from Victoria (Hon. Mr. Ross), whom I regard very kindly, and whose face is usually a picture of repose and kindness-I wonder why that countenance which often reminds me, when the hon. gentleman is half asleep, very much of the Madonna

It is difficult to refrain from calling the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that lie lias three times addressed Mr. Speaker as Mr. Chairman.
Mr. GOURLEY-is so much disturbed. Surely that does not cause that intense ruffling of the spirit which I see depicted in the physiognomy of my hon. friend. It must be the political knife which cuts that lion, gentleman this afternoon. Nothing else could so distort that countenance, which is usually marked by a peaceful, somnolent calm. I was proceeding to say that the association of this clergyman with the government of Canada was either unfortunate for the government or the clergyman-either one or the other.
An lion. MEMBER. Both.
200J

Well, take it that way. There is only one thing to do. The hon. the Minister of the Interior seems to think that this is a little get-up of our friends over here. Let me tell him that there is a bigger get-up from the North-west, if we can believe the reports. Is it not extraordinary news we have had within a day or so from that lovely capital of the North-west; must not my hon. friends from the North-west blush to learn that these colonists, these people, usually so law-abiding, should have been so aroused, that they felt the necessity of taking the law into their own hands, as is done by our friends across the line 1 How these people must have suffered when we find a number of them so aroused as to threaten to resort to lynch law ; and it may possibly happen that these people will become so exasperated that they will break loose from the traditions of the empire, and forget that there are courts in this country where justice is administered. I call upon the government, in the interests of Canada, in the interests of the immigrants, to have the fullest investigation, so that, if they are innocent they can honourably part company with Mr. Barr. I do not know whether the hon. the Minister of the Interior ever met Mr. Barr. I happened to meet him at a hotel in Ottawa this winter, and I must tell you, Sir, at once, that when I heard him talking flippantly, without the slightest sense of propriety, about this movement, I saw at once that the government had made a most serious mistake in having anything to do with him. And when somebody told me he was a clergyman, I was shocked. And soon after upon meeting a person who knew him. this person told me :	' He is a sharper.' And
that is exactly the opinion I formed of the man when I met him at table at the Russell House. If the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock) or the Finance Minister (Hon. Mr. Fielding) had had an interview with him, I am sure they would have had enough knowledge of human nature and enough shrewdness to know that Mr. Barr was not the man to entrust with the honour of Canada-for the ambassador carries the honour of his country-and the government did entrust him with the honour of Canada when they employed him to go up and down England, Scotland and Ireland to represent Canada, to solicit from these people their time and their fortunes to come to Canada and build up this country. Therefore, I hope that the government, in the interest of this great movement, will choose his agents with more discretion. For there is no movement that should be guarded with more care than the immigration movement. We want immigrants. We have territory for millions of people. For my part. I have never failed to do what I could to encourage the immigrant to come to this country, to make him believe that Canada is the fairest home

to be found on the face of this whole earth. I want every man to come to Canada. And no member of my party, thank God, has every said a word against his country. No member of that party has gone up and down throughout the length and breadth of Canada for ten years, as was done by some hon. gentleman opposite, decrying Canada and proclaiming that immigrants should seek a home in any other country on earth but this. I would not stay one hour with a party that would pursue such a policy. Since hon. gentlemen opposite came into power, we on this side have given them a fair chance to do the work the people expect of them. Wherever I am, I proclaim the glories of Canada. I am often criticised for being too intense a Canadian. But I venture to say, that in ten years, the man who loves his country, and uniformly proclaims that love will be in a better position, than the man who hedges, and doubts the possibilities and the future of this country. The young men are coming forward, and will soon be in possession and control of the affairs of Canada, and every young man, I meet, is seized of the idea, of the greatness, the imperial proportions. the magnificent opportunities and potentialities of this beloved Canada.

If the House will extend its courtesy to me for a moment I would like to make a few remarks with regard to matters that have arisen in the course of the debate. In the first place, it is evident that our hon. friends on the other side are under the impression that this colony of people coming from England have been in some way ill treated, subjected to a reception which is likely to discourage other immigrants from coming. I wish.to say that I do not believe that, since the first ship) sailed up the St. Lawrence river, any body of immigrants have come to Canada who have been treated with the same lavish care as that bestowed upon this colony. They have received an amount of attention that no settlers that I ever heard of have received in any part of Canada before. The most elaborate preparations were made by the department, and hon. gentlemen will find, if they will inquire of men upon the ground who are acquainted with the circumstances of the case, that there lias been no attempt in any way whatever to criticise the organization or the work of the department in taking care of these immigrants. We did what never was done before in connection with any party of immigrants-sent out people to put up tents furnished with stoves and put caretakers in attendance. These tents stood twenty miles apart in the colonists' route, so that they might be properly taken care of. The people who settled Manitoba did not have government tents to sleep in. I have seen them in hundreds and thousands going out Mr. GOURLEY.
in their wagons and sleeping under the wagons no matter what the weather was. But, as I say, these colonists were treated with the most elaborate care. And if hon. gentlemen will take the trouble to inquire they will find that every person familiar with the facts of the case will agree with what was stated in a debate in the Northwest Assembly, a copy of which has just been placed in my hands, an extract from which I will read to show that the Immigration Department has done everything which human foresight could devise to provide a proper reception for these immigrants. I quote from the Regina ' Leader ' of July 2nd. Mr. Glinkskill. while attacking Mr. Barr-and, I may say, it seems to be popular to attack Mr. Barr just now- added :
He could not speak too highly of the action of the Immigration Department and the trouble that had been taken by the department. From the time of the arrival of the colonists to the time they were settled on their homesteads the government had done everything in its power.
In addition to doing everything in our power to take care of these people when they arrived and to see that they were transported to their farms, and that their homesteads were found and located for them, we provided farming instructors to teach them the method of putting in and taking care of their crops. So that, so far as that point is concerned, I do not think there is any necessity for defense. But I may add, while I am on this point, that the immigration officials of the government in England are likely to have more trouble in answering the statements of the members of the opposition in this House and elsewhere with regard to the immigration than they are to meet any statements made by members of the Barr colony or any other English settlers in Canada. I object not at all to the statement of my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) or to some of the other statements made. But statements which indicate that English immigrants coining here are ill-treated i r not properly received are; the worst and most difficult to meet on the part of our immigration agents in the old country. The anxiety some of our hon. friends express for the success of immigration would be better shown by refraining from making statements which cannot be justified. Now, a word or two with regard to the promises made or engagements entered into by the government with these people. The government entered into no engagement whatever with these people except that they would give them homesteads within a certain tract of land. They did reserve and give homesteads in that tract to any who wanted them. A considerable number of these people found, as we knew they would find when they came here, that they did not want to take up homesteads in that tract. We did the best we could to find homesteads for them in

other places. It has been stated that a large number have returned to England and have complained of the treatment they received. I have the statement of the oliicsr who is in charge of these people that not a single original Barr colonist has returned to England. That statement was made on the 16th June, about twenty days ago. The statements made in the press in regard to this matter as a rule, are simply wild statements. Our friends on the other side of the House should not take up statements of this kind, assume that they are true and hold the government responsible for the condition of things which they show, making speeches in this House which are taken up in England as made by responsible men
speakername: The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton).

speechtext:
Does the bon. gentleman (Hon. Sir. Sifton) find anything in the paper he read from to contradict statements made by Sir. Haultain.
The	SIINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
What statement ?

The statements presented by him in the legislature.
The	SIINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
What part of it ? Sir. Haultain made a speech

Sir.	CLARKE.	The	whole statement.
Will the hon. Slinister of the Interior read that statement ? I will send him a copy now.
The	SIINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR
(reading)
The Premier said he did not wish to use his position in the House to make charges against Mr. Barr when that gentleman could not be present to reply. At the same time, he thought some remarks on the subject ought to he made and had very properly been made. From conversation he had had with members of the colony on the trail between Saskatoon and Battleford, he was convinced there had been some gross mismanagement in connection with the colony, and something worse than gross mismanagement in certain financial dealings with it. The Dominion government, by allowing Mr. Barr to reserve a certain number cf townships had to that extent recognized the scheme, and it was the duty of that government to have all the charges cleared up by a thorough investigation. He said this was in the interests of the territories and in the interests of some of the best immigrants that ever came into the country.
My hon. friend asked me if I was contradicting Mr. Haultain. I am not prepared to contradict Mr. Haultain. He expressed his opinion and he is entitled to it. Possibly his opinion may he correct, hut the grounds of his opinion have not been laid before me, and therefore, until they have been, I am entitled to entertain my own opinion.

Probably the hon. gentle man did not hear me. He stated to the House that he had received a newspaper
containing a report of the debate, and he read from a paper that Mr. Clinkskill stated that great care and attention had been paid to the immigrants, and I asked him if he found anything in the debate contradicting the assertions made by the premier?

I was referring to the action of the department, and I say the fact is that the department lias done everything it was possible to do on behalf of these immigrants. We have dealt with them in the most careful and considerate way, and my hon. friends on the other side of the House could not, if they desired to do so, lay their finger upon a single thing that ought to have been done which was not done in connection with the arrangements or the reception of these immigrants. Now the point which the hon. gentleman originally drew attention to, and to which I find no fault, is the apparent allegation that there has been financial dealings between members of the colony and Mr. Barr himself, and that Mr. Barr has not dealt properly with them. In so far as that is concerned, as I have already said in reply to the hon. gentleman, I have no information, and can therefore express no opinion. But so far as the relations of the department with these people are concerned, I have to say that we have not been in default in any respect whatever, and that no member of the colony, so far as I know, has stated that the government has been at fault or bas been in default in its dealings with them. My hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, has made a laboured attempt to show that the statement I made in my first remarks regarding the relations between Mr. Barr, the colony, and Mr. Barr and the department, was not correct. I have to repeat that the statement which I made was absolutely correct.
I did not say it was incorrect. All I said was that it did not seem to be quite consistent with the statement of the Commissioner of Immigration.

The hon. gentleman's argument appeared designed to leave upon the minds of the members of the House the impression that my statement was not accurate. I have simply to say that my statement was accurate in every possible respect. I may say en passant that I did not assume, in stating the position as I did, that I am bound by a newspaper report of statements of one of tlie officers of the department, which may or may not be correctly reported. But tire facts are precisely as I have stated, that the relations of the department with Mr. Barr consisted simply in the fact that we reserved certain lands in pursuance of the arrangements which we made with Mr. Barr, and Mr. Barr has riot received any

commission from the Department of the Interior in any way, shape or form, and no agreement exists between the department and Mr. Barr to pay him anything. If Mr. Preston did make any statement that indicated the contrary, his statement was to that extent incorrect. The deputy minister made the arrangement himself, and he informs me that lie refused to make any arrangement for compensation. The only tiling in the world that the department did, so far as Mr. Barr was concerned, was to say, if you secure settlers for these lands before a certain date, we will accept entries for them. Mr. Barr paid his money, he produced his settlers, and they made their entry, and the result is that we have at the present time something over 1,800 homestead entries from good and substantial people, some of the best people, as Mr. Haul-tain said, that ever went into the North-west. As my colonial agent reports, not a single one of these immigrants has returned to England. So I do not see that there is anything unsatisfactory in the nature of the transaction, nor do I see any reason why it should be criticised adversely. It is, no doubt, unfortunate that the financial arrangements between Mr. Barr and the people he brought out turned out as they did. It would be more satisfactory if he had been able to remain with the colony and to close the matter up. But no member of that colony has laid any complaints before the department, no member of the colony has said to the department, we have been misled, we have paid this money for which we .have got no value. Therefore, nothing has been done which would justify the Department of the Interior in ordering an investigation. The position at the present time is that the affair has been successfully carried out. In so far as Mr. Barr and his people are concerned, and the financial arrangements originally entered into between them, if they have been severed, they have been severed voluntarily by the people and Mr. Barr, and Mr. Barr has refunded any money which he may have had that belonged to these people. If, therefore, the position is such that an investigation is demanded, then certainly the information ought to be placed before the department which would justify such an investigation, but up to the present time that has not been done.

With the indulgence of the House, I would like to say one or two words in respect to what has just fallen from the Minister of the Interior. He accused me of having made a laboured statement to show that he was incorrect. I did not make any laboured statement, or any statement at all, to show that he was incorrect, but I brought to his attention, as it was my right and duty to do, the fact that the statement of his chief commissioner of immigration in England was entirely Hon. Mr. SIFTON.
different to that which he made in the House, and entirely different to that which he has made to the House just now. My hon. friend, says he is not responsible for the utterances of Mr. Preston. He is responsible for the utterances of Mr. Preston when Mr. Preston undertakes to speak as commissioner of immigration for Canada.

My hon. friend is now making a statement wholly incorrect. I did not say that I was not responsible for the utterances of Mr. Preston, I said I was not responsible for his reported utterances, which might or might not be correct. If the hon. gentleman wishes to criticise my utterances, he should take the trouble to listen to what I said.

I listened carefully to the hon. gentleman, and I gathered from his statement what I said to the House a moment ago. If he did not mean that, I am glad to know it. I think under the circumstances it would be his duty to communicate at once by telegrain with his chief commissioner in London and find whether that chief commissioner did make a statement which is diametrically opposed to the statement of the Minister of the Interior in the House to-day. That at least is ,due to the House, and due to the country, and to the government of which the hon. gentleman is a member, and more than that, to himself. Now it is a remarkable thing that the chief commissioner of immigration in England should have made this statement, if lie has made it, and we find it reported in the ' Canadian Gazette ' in London, a reputable journal, we find it copied in the 'Westminster Gazette,' another reputable journal, that Mr. Barr was to receive seven shillings apiece for each of these immigrants. My hon. friend does not say that he is not to receive anything.
Yes, I do.
Well, he did not state that to the House.
Yes, I did.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. I marked his words most particularly. He said that his deputy minister had not made any agreement

Not at all, the hon. gentleman is making a statement that is wholly incorrect. I stated as clearly as the English language would allow that there was no such arrangement for the payment of any money to Mr. Barr, and I then followed it up by saying that my deputy minister had so informed me.

Well, I understood the hon. gentleman to say nothing of the kind, but to use the language which I have quoted, and I say that after hearing

liis very emphatic statement made just now
' Hansard ' will show.
I am perfectly aware of that, that is not special news to us. The hon. gentleman is not enlightening us in any way by stating that ' Hansard ' will show. We knew that before he made the remark.
It will enlighten the hon. gentleman when he reads it.

This is, I think, notwithstanding the very flippant way in which the hon. gentleman is disposed to treat it, a matter of some serious concern, because, we have Mr. Preston reported in two leading journals of the mother country as having stated that the government was to pay to Mr. Barr seven shillings per head for these immigrants. We have that published through the length and breadth of the United Kingdom, and if that statement is incorrect which was made as far back as the 28th of May, how does it happen that no contradiction has been made in the ' Canadian Gazette ' or in some leading journal in the mother country ? I suppose the hon. minister's attention or the attention of some of his officials has been drawn to this interview. I would suppose that the officers' in charge of the administration of his department would keep track of information of this kind relating to the Department of the Interior, and I have not the slightest doubt that this came to the attention of some officer of his department, although, of course I accept without the slightest hesitation the statement of the hon. gentleman that he knew of it for the first time to-day. If we have a right to assume that, how does it happen that up to this time uot the slightest contradiction of Mr. Preston's statement has been made ? How does it happen that no officer of the Department of the Interior has called the attention of Mr. Preston to the fact that he has made a very serious and misleading statement in the press of the mother country and which is to be found in the newspaper which I have just read to the House ? The hon. minister thinks that the opposition are to be censured for bringing this matter to the attention of the gov-'ernment. that we ought to apologize, as has been suggested, for bringing the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that one of his officers is reported as publishing through a leading paper in the mother country a statement diametrically opposed to that which he has given to the House to-day. I should think the hon. gentleman would be glad to have his attention called to the subject in order that he might tell Mr. Tres-ton that the statement made by him was a statement that had no foundation in fact. Instead of that he seems to be a little pettish on the subject, a little irritable, and he talks about the attempts made to show that what he has said is incorrect. Some one is incorrect. There is no doubt that either Mr. Preston is incorrect or the hon. minister is incorrect, and we assume in the House, of course, taking the hon. gentleman's statement, that it is Mr. Preston who is incorrect. I say that if Mr. Preston is incorrect the sooner he Is corrected the better, because the hon. gentleman cannot conceal from the people of this country the fact that there has been a great deal of scandal in connection with this immigration, and when coupled with that we have the fact that the people of the British Isles are infcrmed that Mr. Barr was in the pay of this government I do not think it is necessary for the hon. gentleman to show the pettishness lie has done in regard to this matter or the spirit in which he has dealt with it in making the speech which he has just made to this House. I think it is of importance to this country that incorrect statements should not be published in the mother country by Mr. Preston acting as chief commissioner of the Canadian government in respect to immigration. I repeat that statement. I withdraw nothing from it. I say that in bringing this matter to the attention of the House my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) has done no more than his duty and now that these facts have been brought to his attention he would have failed absolutely in his duty as a public man and as a member of this House if he had not brought this matter to the attention of this House and the country.

Did I understand the hon. minister to make the statement that the department have received 1,800 homestead entries from the Barr colonists ?
The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR, I will give my hon. friend (Mr. Bell) the number in a moment-it is 1823.
Mi-. BELL. Now, the deputy minister in giving evidence in the course of this session before the Committee on Agriculture said-
I would call the attention of the hon. member (Mr. Beil) to the fact that he has already spoken.
I think several other hon. gentlemen have already spoken.
I would prefer to give the hon. gentleman the information if he wishes to ask for it.

The statement was made by Mr. Smart, Deputy Minister of the Interior before the Committee on Agriculture that out of 1,500 or 1,600 entries, only about 500 of these colonists had settled in the colony and on the adjacent lands.
When was that statement made ?

On the 3rd of June, 1903.

The MINISTER OB' THE INTERIOR. I suppose they have been making entries since that time ?
The deputy minister claimed that up to that time they had made some 1,500 or 1,000 entries.

We have received from the people who came in Mr. Barr's party altogether, according to the returns that were furnished to me yesterday, 1,823 entries, but of course ihey are not all on the reserve. They were made at different places. If they decided to go elsewhere we facilitate them in doing so.

The information was furnished by the department to me yesterday.
Could the hon. minister lay that on the Table ?
Yes, if the hon. gentleman desires it.

I do not wish to take up the time of the House, but I would just call the attention of the House to what Air. Preston is reported to have said in the ' Canadian Gazette ' from which the hon. leader of the opposition (Sir. Borden, Halifax) has quoted. I understood the hon. leader of the opposition to allege that the statement of Mr. Preston was that Mr. Barr was to receive from the Canadian government seven shillings per head for the immigrants he brought to Canada.
speakername: The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Hon. Sir William Mulock).

speechtext: I read his statement and I read it seven shillings per head. He said the amount had not been finally settled. I read the exact words.

The hon. gentleman read the statement and commented upon it and in his comment he ventured to depart from the statement. I merely wish to emphasize the fact that his comment suggesting that Mr. Preston had stated that the government intended to pay seven shillings per head is not borne out by the quotation. The hon. gentleman pretended to suggest that there was some conflict of statement between the hon. Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton) and Mr. Preston inasmuch as the hon. Minister of the Interior had laid it down beyond any question there was no foundation for Ihe statement that Mr. Barr was to be paid by the Canadian government seven shillings per head or anything per head, and that Mr. Preston's statement was at variance with the statement of the hon. minister. That is the suggestion of the hon. leader of the opposition and his suggestion is a development of the statement of Mr. Preston. His comment and inference are far greater Mr. BELL.
than are warranted by the statement of Mr. Preston. I find that Mr. Preston said at the most, according to the report ' he will also probably receive ' not that he will receive, but that * he will also probably receive ' and then it goes on to say [DOT] the matter has not yet been settled.'
Read the whole of it.

Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) permit me to read it ? I am trying to read the report of his statement. ' He will also probably receive-the matter has not yet been settled-seven shillings per emigrant from the Canadian government.' Then, the hon. leader of the opposition, forgetting that Mr. Preston said that he would 'probably' receive and forgetting that Mr. Preston said the matter had not been settled proce ds to attribute to Mr. Preston the positive statement that the government had promised to pay seven shillings per head. That is something that an officer 3,000 miles away cannot know and that is the way such a qualified statement as this can be developed in a few moments into a positive allegation. Surely the hon. leader of the opposition is forgetting that at a meeting of the Com-m'ttee on Agriculture to which the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) alluded the Deputy Minister of the Interior was examined. I was not present at that meeting, but I am told that the deputy minister was examined on that question and upon that question he stated in the most explicit language that the government had not agreed to pay Mr. Barr any money per head for these colonists and that that statement of Air. Smart was duly reported in the press of Canada. And yet in the face of that, and the qualified doubting statement of an officer, the leader of the opposition pretends to allege that a certain sum must have been agreed upon to be paid. That is not a fair argument for the leader of the opposition to make, and a closer regard to accuracy would give much greater weight to any argument that may be advanced for the enlightenment of this House or the country.

It is rather amusing to find the Alinister of the Interior adopting the tone he has adopted in lecturing hon. gentlemen on this side of the House for making any criticism whatever of anything that occurs in his department. Has the Department of the Interior during the hon. gentleman's incumbency of office been conducted in such a manner as to preclude criticism ? Has not the air been full of rumours too with respect to mismanagement in the Yukon? Is there not now a commission appointed to investigate into the affairs of the Yukon : have not the newspapers for several months past beeii full of complaints with respect to this Barr colony? And yet we are not to mention the matter here because we are told it is going to have a serious effect upon immigration into

this country. Why, Sir, Premier Haultain of the North-west Territories made a stronger j statement in the North-west Assembly. He having met these colonists on their trek from Saskatoon to Battleford; having talked to them and having heard their complaints, lie the premier of that country says that these are grave charges against tliis government, and that in the interest of the country these charges should be investigated. Mr. Haultain very clearly and very distinctly connects the government with Mr. Barr in this matter. I believe that it is in the interest of truth and it should be stated that after the mischief had been done, after this man Barr had been sent as an agent to England and allowed to make all sorts of wild and gross misstatements in regard to the conditions that the immigrants would find in Canada ; after all this had been done and the people were brought here, I do believe that the department made an honest effort to try and make the conditions as easy for these immigrants as possible. I was in Winnipeg and visited the immigration office there and I am satisfied from the statements to me that the officers were doing honestly what they could to make things as easy for these immigrants as possible. But the mischief had already been done, and it was not the officers at Winnipeg who were to blame, but it was the officers higher placed in the department who made this arrangement, Mr. Preston made his statement which appeared in the ' Cana-ian Gazette' on the 28th of May at the very time when the Minister of the Interior was In London, and I have no doubt he was in daily communication with his officer Mr. Preston, and I have no doubt that he read the 'Canadian Gazette.' It is a sort of quasi government organ, I believe, and it is looked upon of course as speaking with authority on Canadian matters in England and I assume the minister read the statement. At all events he should have read it and in the absence of any contrary statement I believe he did.

I stated in reply to the leader of the opposition and I state now that my attention was never called to the interview in question until this afternoon. I was in London at the time I believe. I did not occupy much of my time in reading newspapers, but whether I did or not I did not see that interview and I never saw the statements contained in it until now.

It may be that the minister's social duties were.so great as to deprive him of the opportunity of reading the newspapers, and of course I must accept the statement that he did not see the interview in question. But Mr. Preston must have seen the interview and he has not contradicted it, and therefore we must take it for granted that the interview represents
exactly what Mr. Preston said. The Minister of the Interior, as he has admitted, is responsible for the statements of his agent Mr. Preston. Mr. Preston of course gave us the impression last year that he was as big a man as the Minister of the Interior himself.
An understudy.

Yes a sort of understudy to the minister. At all events it is perfectly true that the Minister of the Interior cannot divest himself of the responsibility for whatever failure there may be in connection with this Barr colony. Mr. Preston says in his uncontradicted statement that they were in constant communication with Mr. Barr from the outset, and on the 28th of May, long after the immigrants had shown themselves to be thoroughly dissatisfied with Mr. Barr's leadership and had repudiated him and driven him out of the colony ; even after that, Mr. Preston the responsible head of the immigration office in London states that they were perfectly satisfied with Mr. Barr. Therefore they would make Mr. Barr their agent even by that endorsation alone, so that the department is absolutely responsible for everything this man Barr lias done. The complaint we make is that they took this man up without knowing anything of his character, and without taking precautions that he would not make statements to the immigrants which were grossly misleading, and induce them to come here under false pretenses. And now the minister insinuates that we are unpatriotic because we draw the attention of the country to the misconduct of the Department of the Interior in this respect. If we had no other justification, the statement that is made by Mr. Haultain the Premier of the North-west Territories, is sufficient in itself. He says:-
Read it again.
It cannot be read too often and I should think that the member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) would have interest enough in that country from which he comes
He has got all he can.
I have not got as much as you have yet; you better sing small.

These railways that the member for Saskatchewan has in that country would not be much good to him if there is a black eye given, to immigration. Mr. Haultain says :
From conversations he had with members of the colony on the trail between Saskatoon and Battleford he was convinced there had been gross mismanagement.
That is strong language coming from the premier of the Territories. Gross mismanagement by whom ? Was it by Mr Barr ? Well, if it be. Mr. Barr is the accredited agent of the Department of the Interior ac-

A message was delivered by,the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, as follows :
His Excellency the Governor General desires the immediate attendance of your honourable House in the Senate Chamber.
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, with the House, went to the Senate chamber.
And having returned,

I have the honour to inform the House that when the House did attend His Excellency the Governor General in the Seuate Chamber, His Excellency was pleased to give, in His Majesty's name, the Royal Assent to the following Bills :

An Act respecting the Quebec Bridge Company. and to change its name to ' The Quebac Bridge and Railway Company.'
An Act respecting the Vancouver and Kootenay Railway Company.
An Act to confer on the Commissioner of Patents certain powers for the relief of James S. McDougall.
An Act respecting the London and Port Stanley Railway Company.
An Act respecting the Rocky Mountain Railway and Coal Company.
An Act to incorporate the New Canadian Company, Limited.
An Act to amend chapter 27 of the revised statutes, respecting the Department of Public Printing and Stationery.
An Act respecting and restricting Chinese Immigration.
An Act to -amend the Customs Act.
An Act to provide for further advances to the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal.
An Act respecting certain aid for the extension of the Canadian Northern Railway.
An Act to incorporate the Lumberman's Fire Insurance Company.
