An Act for granting to His Majesty the certain sums of money for the public service of the financial years ending respectively, 30th June, 1903. and the 30tli June, 1904.

['In accordance with the agreement referred to, I beg to move:\nProvided always that the location of the line of railway to be built by the company hereby incorporated shall not at any point be nearer than five miles from the line of railway now or hereafter built or located by the Quebec and New Brunswick Railway Company except with the consent of the latter company or of the Governor General in Council.']

When interrupted by the summons of the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod. I was referring to the statement >
made by the bon. the Minister of Labour

and his attempt to prove that the hon. the leader of the opposition drew a wrong inference from the Preston Interview. That interview we must accept as authentic. The proof of its authenticity is beyond all question. Mr. Preston says :
He will also probably receive-the matter has not yet been settled-seven shillings per immigrant from the Canadian government.
The only inference, Mr. Speaker, that can be drawn from that statement is that an amount was to be paid, but what that amount was to be had not yet been settled. Mr. Preston speaks in another place :
It being the custom to pay to agents obtaining immigrants a certain percentage per head.
I think that is what the department does when immigrants are brought from the United States. The agents are allowed $3 per head, and evidently this man was to get a certain amount, probably seven shillings per head. It may be that now, on account of these complaints, the government will not pay him anything. Certainly they should not, under the circumstances. 1 fail to understand why the hon. the Minister of the Interior should have thought fit to censure hou. members on this side for bringing this matter up. Why, we would be remiss in our duty if we did not ; we would lay ourselves open to censure for having failed to do our duty. I find in the Toronto 'News' of July 9th, the following despatch from Winnipeg :
As to his future plans, Mr. Barr was noncommittal. saying these were yet indefinite but it was possible he might bring out more immigrants.
So well satisfied apparently was the government with Mr. Barr that he is on the point of bringing out more immigrants. Yet, we are to be censured by the hon. the Minister of the Interior for venturing to criticise this tiling in the House. The hon. the minister would evidently like to be in the position of the Czar of all the Russias, against whom, when he issues an edict, no man dare say a word. That might suit the hon. gentleman, and he might find it convenient to put the country under martial law. The hon. gentleman will have to look after the newspapers, for they are committing the unpardonable sin of daring to criticise the conduct of his own department. Unquestionably this is a matter that should have, as Mr. Haultaiu says, a most thorough investigation. It is incumbent on the Department of the Interior to clear itself of these charges, because the charges made against Mr. Barr are actually made against the Department of the Interior, which made him its agent. Could there be any doubt in any man's mind as to the agency existing between Mr. Barr and the Department of the Interior ? What are the facts ? This man Barr, before he did anything at all. went to the Department of the Interior and arranged to have a block of homesteads reserved for him and his colony. Then he went to the Canadian Pacific Railway and got a reserve of certain lands adjoining these homesteads. Then, from the very inception of this scheme, Mr. Barr was in constant communication with the government. The government knew everything that was going on, and approved of his plans. The government insisted upon knowing all about the character of the immigrants he was bringing in. Mr. Preston said :
In granting this concession to Mr. Barr, our government had no intention of divesting itself of its responsibility.
But they had the same responsibility as if Mr. Preston himself, or any other agent in the employ of the department, had got up that colony. Mr. Preston said : 1 We do not wish to divest ourselves of any responsibility.' The hon. the Minister of the Interior to-day, however, declines to assume any responsibility. Mr. Preston further said :
The immigrants paid their entrance fees to the homesteads through myself, and so perfect was our organization that not an hour's delay at any point, not even at Winnipeg, from which came such disquieting news some time ago, was experienced in passing through.
We know better than that. We know that it was a long time before these people could be moved. We know that there was a great deal of trouble and difficulty while they were camped at Saskatoon, and that no proper arrangements were made for their removal. They were told by Mr. Barr-and that must have been with the knowledge of Mr. Preston, because he says the government were perfectly cognizant of everything connected with the transaction-that houses would be ready for them and that teams would be on band to carry them from Saskatoon to their homesteads, and that a certain amount of ploughing had beep done. Not one of these houses were built, and tents had to be provided for these people when they arrived at their destination. The statement of Mr. Preston, therefore, with respect to the arrangements made, is absolutely untrue. After these people were dumped down by Mr. Barr, in Saskatoon, the department did take hold of them and do what it could under the circumstances, it is not for what the department did for these people, after they were dumped at Saskatoon, that we are criticising it, but because the hon. minister anil his officers were not aware that this was simply a money making scheme of Mr. Barr, and'that lie was gulling these people all through. A considerable number of those colonists were certainly not suited to agricultural life at all, and had not the slightest conception of wliat it meant. Some of them had never been outside the city of London, except on Hampstead Hill. I do not see how the government can escape responsibility, and we demand an investigation, in order to have

tliose responsible brought to account. Instead of its being an injury to the country to have this matter criticised, it will be for the good of the country to show the outside world that when there is anything wrong we are willing to investigate and make it right. It is the bounden duty of the hon. minister to see that a thorough investigation be made at once by a responsible party, and that compensation be given those who have been wronged, and punishment be meted out to the guilty.

The opposition may congratulate themselves upon the fact that they have kicked up quite a disturbance, which they think, perhaps, may have the effect of interfering with the good work that is being done by the Minister of the Interior in promoting immigration. I quite sympathize with the opposition. They have been fishing all session, and up to the present time they have been able to catch nothing. But they think now they have hooked a small minnow
A bar.

They think they have got a little fish in the shape of this trouble they have made this afternoon. The whole thing is a tempest in a teapot, and they have gone far afield to connect Mr. Barr with the gov-'ernment in this immigration scheme. I am not going to discuss any of the statements made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) who has just taken his seat, nor the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Gourley). But I do think the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), who occupies a very responsible position in this House has gone a little far afield in trying to misquote the statements made by the Minister of the Interior. and also the statements made in the 'Canadian Gazette' as to what Mr. Preston said in the old country. The leader of the opposition made the positive statement that the government had agreed to give Mr. Barr seven shillings for each immigrant that he brought out. and that Mr. Preston said so. He never said anything of the kind
I beg the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Davis) pardon. I read exactly what Mr. Preston did say.

I accept the statement of the hon. gentleman. But it appears to jne that it was as clear as the English language could make it that Mr. Preston did not say what has keen attribued to him, but he said that the matter had not been settled but they might probably give seven shillings a head. However, as I said, the whole case is a tempest in a teapot. I would like to review the whole case.
Oh. oh.

I am interested in this matter, and I venture to say I know as much about it, and perhaps a good deal more, than some of the hon. gentlemen who have Mr. FOWLER.
been speaking on the other side. I am in communication all the time with the gentlemen connected with the colonists. I met Mr. Barr When he arrived with his colony at St. John, and all the colonists that I spoke to were well seized of the fact that the government had nothing to do with Mr. Barr, that he was going on his own responsibility, and had no connection with the government. This Mr. Barr, an English clergyman, came to the department and said he intended to bring out a colony of Englishmen. Of course, we are anxious, as hon. gentlemen opposite are anxious, to get English immigrants into Canada. The department treated Mr. Barr courteously and set aside a certain quantity of land for the colonists he intended to bring in. Mr. Barr brought the colonists in and the government had nothing to do with him, but they did all they could to facilitate the settlement of these colonists. That is proven by the gentleman who brought this question up in the North-west assembly, Mr. Cliukskill. He stated that the government had done everything they could to make things easy for the colonists on their arrival in Canada. This gentleman, Mr. Olinkskill, who started all this disturbance, is a strong Conservative. If he could have made out anything against the government he would have been glad to do it. But he declared in the assembly that the government and its officials had done.everything possible for these colonists. And Air. Haultain made a statement, he made no charge, but simply a rambling statement in reply to Mr. Clinkskill and suggested that the ease should be investigated. What is there to investigate ? The government is not concerned in the matter so far as I can see, except that they did what they could to facilitate the settlement of these people in Canada. Some of the statements made by hon. gentlemen opposite may have the effect of checking the stream of immigration to this country. So far as the people of the North-west are 'concerned, they will not thank these gentlemen for the statements they have made this afternoon. One gentleman, for instance, said that the Barr colony had not proven a success. As a matter of fact it is a success. The fact that Air. Barr as head of the colony has been ousted, to use the common expression, does not prove that the colony is not successful. I have a letter from Air. Lloyd, who is in charge of the colony, and he assures me that the colonists are doing all right, making their entries and going ahead. If there were any charges to be made, Air. Lloyd would probably be the man to make them. If there had been anything unpleasant, would not he have written to the minister cr somebody else asking for an investigation ? But there is nothing in his letters about these gentlemen having been swindled out of their money by Air. Barr. He wrote to me that the colonists wanted a post office. The Postmaster General sent up an inspector

to look over the situation, and the result is that they have their post office. They get everything they ask for. The Minister of the Interior has even sent up a sub-agent to receive their entries, so that they may not have to drive sixty or seventy miles to make them. The colonists have nothing against the government; they are not grumbling at all. There may be some grumbling in connection with Mr. Barr,.but Mr. Barr and the government are separate people. If when Mr. Barr, an English clergyman, came here to Ottawa and said he was organizing a colony of British immigrants, the minister had not treated him as he did, and if he had not set aside these lands, what a howl would have been raised by hon. gentlemen opposite. They would have raised a debate lasting even longer than this one, and would have declared that we did not approve of British immigrants, that no immigrants would suit us, but Doukhobors and Galicians and so on. as they have said over and over again. The Immigration Department, under the control of the lion. Minister of the Interior has proved most successful. It makes hon. gentlemen opposite sore to And that 120.000 good immigrants were brought into this country last year, particularly when they contrast this with the feeble efforts put forth by their own friends when they were in office. These hon. gentlemen are always looking for a weak point in this government, but, so far as what they have been talking about this afternoon is concerned, there is very little capital in it all for them. Why did Mr. Clinkskill bring this matter up in the territorial assembly ? Hon. gentlemen opposite read the newspapers, so they must have been made aware that when Mr. Barr got to Saskatoon, he and ' r. Clink-skill had a falling out which nearly, ended in a free fight. Mr. Clinkskill would naturally feel a little sore; so lie, went down to the meeting of the assembly and made these statements against Mr. Barr. There was not a word, mark you, against the government though Mr. Clinkskill is a strong Conservative. Mr. Haultain answered in a general way that there should be an investigation. There is nothing in that; he makes no charges. And now hon. gentlemen opposite take it up and make it the subject of half a day's debate in the hope that they may be able to show that there is something wrong and that they may stop immigration coming into the country. They c uld occupy their time more profitably in discussing other subjects. No doubt, what they have said will make good newspaper articles for their press, and it will be wired across to Britain to make sensational articles there. So far as the benefit of Canada is concerned, these hon. gentlemen opposite are not doing a friendly act, and they are very far' from helping us to settle the prairies of the west.

The hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) seems to think that the opposition have done
something wrong in bringing this matter before the House, and characterizes the conduct of hon. gentlemen on this side as raising a tempest in a teapot. Is that what he calls the remarks of the premier of the territories made in the legislative assembly a few days ago ? Has he no respect for the high position of Mr. Haultain and the views he expressed, that he should characterize this as a tempest in a teapot ?

I want to tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) that no doubt the premier of the North-west Territories is trying to assist hon. gentlemen opposite to kick up some kind of a disturbance. He is doing it all the time.

Mr. Haultain made a statement in reference to facts that came under his own observation. He said he had received information at first hand, and therefore he was justified in making the grave charges which he did, charges of financial mismanagement, even of crookedness.
Did Mr. Haultain, in his speech in the assembly, say that the government was connected directly or indirectly with any of these financial transactions 7

He said that the government's connection with it demanded a searching inquiry, in the interests of immigration and in the interests of the Northwest Territories, so as either to substantiate the charges or disprove them. Yet the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis>
says it is only a tempest in a teapot.
The colony were well pleased with the fact that the government had nothing to do with Mr. Barr.

Where did they so express themselves, and when 7 It was not in the provinces, because we never saw anything to that effect. But they associated the Rev. Mr. Barr with the operations carried on by the government, and does the member for Saskatchewan take the ground that there was no connection between Mr. Barr and the government ? No connection after Mr. Barr had succeeded in getting the government to set apart several townships of land for the purpose of enabling him to colonize it. and to get a commission for so doing, for the purpose of enabling him to get a rake-off out of it. under the garb of philanthropy, when bringing people from the old country here under misrepresentation and delusion 7 Yet vre are told that it is only a tempest in a teapot. He says the Barr colony wras a great success, and he says that in face of the fact that we are told by a reporter from that country that only 500 out of the 2,000 have settled in that colony. What became of the other 1,500 7 They were like the children of Israel who wandered forty years in the wilderness, and when they got to the promised land very few were remaining of those who left their homes. Then it was

not an unqualified success. These men discovered, when they reached the promised land which was represented to them as a land flowing with milk and honey, that they had been misled and deceived. The Minister of the Interior says he thinks it is a very improper thing that the opposition should bring this matter to the attention of the House and the country. Why, if nothing else was accomplished in bringing this matter to the attention of the minister than to give him an opportunity of knowing what he did not know before, which he admits himself he did not know, I say if nothing else was accomplished but to enable him to contradict the allegations which were made in the ' Canadian Gazette ' in. London, then we are justified in bringing it before the House. He declared that the statements that appeared in the ' Gazette ' were incorrect in almost every particular, but he admits that he had not seen these statements, and knew nothing of them until they were brought to Ills attention in the House to-day. So, if nothing else was accomplished than to give him an opportunity of denying these statements it certainly justifies us in doing what we have done. In my judgment there is nothing more detrimental to the country, or to the interests of immigration, than to allow the people who come here to be misled. Is it a fact that these people were or were not misled ? Take their own statements for it. What are a few of their statements ? They declare that they were fold that they were coming to a country where they would have a railway at their door, and they find there is no railway within a hundred miles of them. Were they not misled in that particular ? This is their own public statement, made to the whole world, that they were told they were coming to a country where they would have the convenience of a railway at their door; they were going to be planted on land as rich as could be found anywhere in the World; they were going to enter into the enjoyment of homes prepared for them by Mr. Barr and the Canadian government; they were going to enjoy the comforts of life, teams were to be provided for them, the necessaries of life provided for them, some ploughing done. They were brought out in the spring of the year so that they might sow their grain and be ready for reaping it in a few months hence. Yet in all these respects they were the victims of a delusion and a snare-no soil broken up, no homes built, no teams provided, no railway for hundreds of miles of the locality where they were settled. Is it to be said that we are doing wrong in trying to set this matter right ? I ask the question again. Did the Rev. Mr. Barr mislead these people ? Who is the Rev. Mr. Barr ? He is one of the governments agents 1 Under whose aegis was he acting ? Under the aegis of the Department of the Interior,

under the aegis of the government. Very naturally these poor immigrants would say that this man must be regarded as a respectable and a truthful man, otherwise he would not be employed by the Canadian government. Therefore they have a right to assume that the representations he made were correct. Now, I say the very fact that he was acting under the government, under Mr. Preston, the immigration agent, that he was acting with the knowledge and consent of the government, was calculated to mislead these people into relying on his statements. If these statements were correct, there could be no harm done, but if the statements were incorrect, and these people were induced to come to this country through misrepresentation, then I say this government must be held responsible, and the Minister of the Interior must share that responsibility.
The colonists make no such claim.
The colonists declare they were deceived.
By whom ?
By the Rev. Air. Barr, and the Rev. Mr. Barr was an agent of the government, and they had a right to assume that the government would not send out an agent there that would mislead them.
I venture to say there is not one colonist who claims that Air. Barr was tire government agent.
I saw a statement that appeared in one of the western papers, a statement made by one of the colonists, who deliberately claimed that they were deceived.
Not by a government agent ?

By Mr. Barr, and I say Mr. Barr was a government agent, he was acting under the government, acting with the knowledge of the government, he got land set apart for that purpose from the government, he was given the duty of colonizing that land, and was given a rake-off that was going to him for his philanthropic work. So the hon. gentleman should restrain himself.
Air. Barr never got any land from the government in any shape or form.
Did he not get a portion of the land to be set apart to be colonized ?

No.
Alt'. SPROULE. The minister himself stated that the department assigned a certain number of townships to him.

I presume the hon. gentleman would like

639S
to know the facts. Tlie homestead law permits any person over eighteen years of age, and possessing certain qualifications, to take up a homestead, and that is done under the direction of the Minister of the Interior, and I consented to an arrangement whereby a certain number of quarter sections were hold in the names of persons whose names Mr. Barr had furnished to the department, and they were permitted to take up these homesteads.
Does the hon. Minister of the Interior not admit that a certain number of sections were reserved and for what purpose ? For Barr's colonists ?
For homesteading.
For homesteading by Barr's colonists.
For homesteading.

What does the premier of the North-west Territories say ?
The Dominion government, by allowing Mr. Barr to reserve a certain number of townships-
Who allowed him to reserve these townships ? Who had the right or power to give him authority to reserve them ? They would not have been reserved if the hon. Minister of the Interior had not reserved them, and if the authority had not gone out from the Department of the Interior, under the Land Act there could not have been a quarter section reserved anywhere.
That is not disputed. I say the land w;i s not given to Mr. Barr. I say it was given for homesteading.
I do not hear what the hon. minister says.
I said that Mr. Barr did not get the land, the land was reserved for homesteaders who took it up and got it.

The land was reserved for the homesteaders that Mr. Barr was to take there. Suppose I had gone up there as a homesteader, could I have taken up laud In that locality ? I was told that people wTent up into that locality and were not allowed to get a homestead there.

My hon. friend is quite wrong because we did reserve a certain proportion of homesteads for miscellaneous settlers who might go to that locality. We reserved one-quarter section because we knew certain persons might go in there, and being of a somewhat turbulent nature, like my hon. friend, they might desire to make trouble if they could not get land there.

Is that not an admission that there was a reservation made for Mr. Barr ? You reserved out of the reservation for Mr. Barr a certain proportion for the public. The rest of the reservation was for Mr. Barr, who is going in there with tlie authority of the government. What did Mr. Haultain say :
The Dominion government, by allowing Mr. Barr to reserve a certain number of townships had to that extent recognized the scheme.
They recognized the scheme by their own act in reserving that land for Sir. Barr, and they enabled Mr. Barr to mislead the colony and to deceive the people who came out, for the purpose of making the rake-off that he got out of it. What are the statements that these people make ? They say that Mr. Ban- told them that each man must provide himself with a tent or he would provide it, for which he would make a charge of $10. That was not part of the contract entered into with the party when they left England. They rebelled against that lie-cause it was said that these tents would cost them $500, whereas they were to be provided by Barr. Was that statement correct or incorrect ? If that statement was incorrect, and if these colonists were misled to that extent, then the hon. Minister of the Interior should be thankful for having the matter called to his attention so as to give them an opportunity of setting the matter right, of clearing the suspicion that attaches to his department in connection with the transaction, and of making the responsibility rest where it should rest.
If my hon. friend will permit me, hon. gentlemen have my most profound gratitude.

Well, I think there will be more than the hon. gentleman who will be grateful for what has been done here to-day. The poor deceived Barr colonists will be grateful for it, because they will know that somebody has to account for the nefarious transactions that were carried on and under the aegis of the government when they were misled into coming from their homes thousands of miles to settle here. What object had Barr in view which induced him to prosecute this pilanthropic work ? Was it pure philanthropy ? Because he was a minister of the gospel, one would naturally suppose that it was, but the facts that were brought to light afterwards showed that it was not pure philanthropy, that there was a good deal of selfishness in it, and that it was the profits that were being looked for. Who were interested in these profits ? I was wondering in reading over the statement made by Mr. Preston, that it is customary to allow seven shillings per head for these men, although the hon. minister says Barr is not going to be allowed anything, whether there was any party outside of Barr receiving a portion of the prospective rake-off. That is a question

which the hon. minister is hound to set at rest by a proper inquiry. If those under his authority are implicated in it, ail the worse, and the sooner it is known, the better. It is evident that Barr understood that ' he was to receive that amount and that he would receive emoluments from other sources ; otherwise he would not have acted as he did.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before you proceed with this Bill, I wish to state with respect to the amendment of which I gave the necessary notice and which appears upon the Order paper, that I may not find it necessary to move it. I have no objection to the Bill going on, as I understand there has been an agreement come to by which the promoters of this Bill will move an amendment that will satisfy the Quebec and New Brunswick Railway Company. Therefore, with the consent of the House the Bill may proceed, and that amendment can be moved at the end of clause 7. With that understanding I have no objection to the Bill going on.
On section 7,

subsubtopic: QUEBEC, NEW BRUNSWICK AND NOVA SCOTIA RAILWAY COMPANY.

When you left the Chair at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was asking the question: What object had the Rev. Mr. Barr in view of taking up this apparently philanthropic work ? The fact that heretofore he had been .a minister of the gospel would naturally suggest to one's mind his desire to do good to humanity, and from the promptings of a generous and Christian nature he might have been induced to embark upon such an enterprise for the good of his fellowman without any expectation of a worldly return to himself. Had that been the case one would have been reluctant to believe many of the unfavourable accounts that have been given of Mr. Barr's operations during the time he -was bringing these people to the country; but if we examine into it to ascertain whether he might not have been prompted by some selfishly lucrative object, I think we will come to the eonclnsion that unless there was a profit somewhere or other he would not have engaged in the enterprise. Now, from whom was lie likely to receive the profit, if profit he expected. We are told that he got $6 a head for the immigrants as commission from the steamship company, and if he had nothing more than that it would give him S12.000 ou two thousand people, which in itself would be a very substantial salary for a year's operations. It may be said that the Rev. Mr. Barr was obliged to undergo very large expense. I claim that this cannot be because so far as the emigration part of it was concerned, it was practically done by the chief emigration agent in England. W. T. R. Preston. Although Mr. Barr gathered up this large crowd, he was not under great expense while doing so. Now, if the surmise of W. T. R. Preston he correct, that Mr. Barr was to get seven shillings each for the immigrants, and I have no doubt that the understanding come to between him and Preston was to that effect, then he would realize $3,500 from that source and that would give him $15,500. That would be a pretty comfortable return for a year's operations. But in addition to that we are told that Mr. Barr compelled these poor people to buy tents from him for which he charged $10 apiece. The minister of the Interior told us that this colony was taken in hand by the Emigration Department from the time they were gathered together in England until they were lauded at their destination in the North-west. The expenses in this connection were borne by the Canadian government and not by Mr. Barr. It is said that Mr. Barr purchased these tents for less than $5, and. therefore, supposing that they bought 1.000 tents, he had a clear rake-off of $5 apiece, or $5,000

in all. Therefore, he must have been in $20,500 for bis business operations for the year. This was a pretty good compensation to him for the work he was supposed to have undertaken for the sake of philanthropy. When we find a minister of the gospel abandoning his religious calling and taking up a work of this kind for an apparently philanthrophic motive, and when we find that there is a profit coming out of the business, we will have to seek for some other real aim on his part than the humanitarian.
He says that he is out of pocket $10,000.

There were a great many statements made by the Rev. Mr. Barr which were declared by those colonists to be absolutely untrue. How do we know whether this is true or false ? But we do know that he got six dollars a head from the steamship companies, which was $12,000, and that there was some understanding between him and Sir. Preston that he was to get some kind of rake-off from the department.
Did he get it ?

I am not saying whether he got it or not. The Slinister of the Interior denies that he got it. But there was an understanding that he was to get something from that source, whether he got it or not. Then, if it be a fact, as it was publicly stated by .one of the Barr colonists, that he compelled them to buy a thousand tents at ten dollars apiece, which could be purchased anywhere at five dollars apiece, he made something out of that. These statements, so far as 1 know, have not been successfully contradicted by Mr. Barr, and, therefore, I have a. right to assume that there must be some truth in them. So that it is quite clear that it was not on account of his philanthropy that this gentleman took up this work. I am afraid we are obliged to conclude that it was the mercenary nature lie possesses, the disposition to make . money, the love of filthy lucre, the almighty dollar, and the broad acre, that induced him to go into this scheme. There may be some other sources from which he was to receive returns that we know nothing about. The government tell us tliat they reserved a certain number of sections of this land. For what purpose ? Was it to be sold to Mr. Barr after he colonized the district ? What arrangement had he with- the Canadian Pacific Railway Company ? I have no doubt that he was quite sharp enough as a business man to make as good a bargain with the railway company as he made with the government. How do we know that he had not an understanding with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to purchase land from them at $3 an acre ? If he planted these colonists on the odd-numbered sec-201
tions, the value of this other land would be enhanced, and would rapidly run up to $5 an acre. Very likely he would have the extra profits resulting from that. Then he may have purchased other sections from the government, either directly or through his friends. I have no doubt that if a careful inquiry were made, we would find other sources besides those which we know about, whereby the Rev. Mr. Barr expected to make large sums of money; because lie seems to be exactly that kind of character -a man who has abandoned his religious calling and gone into this business under the guise of philanthropy and sympathy for the down-trodden, with the deliberate purpose of deceiving the people. I say that we may reasonably come to the conclusion that there are other bad features of his conduct that have not been brought to light, and that can only be ascertained by an inquiry. Whether that inquiry should be by commission or otherwise I am not prepared to say ; but I agree with Mr. Haultain that the matter is too glaringly suspicious and irregular to be allowed to pass over in silence ; and the Department of the Interior must lie under the odium that attaches to their connection with the transaction unless they clear it up in some way or other.
The next question to ask, the answer to which would be interesting if we could ascertain it, is, who were his associates ? I have no doubt that practically the Rev. Mr. Barr was only a stool pigeon. There are many transactions in which there are silent and sleeping partners, who share in the profits and cover up their tracks as best they can ; and it would be interesting to know whether the Rev. Mr. Barr had any associates, or whether he got all the profits himself. How much did he make out of this transaction ? To what extent was he supported in it by the Minister of the Interior and the Immigration Department ? We do know this, that these 2,000 immigrants, whom the Minister of the Interior tells us were brought by Mr. Barr, and the bringing of whom the government had nothing to do with, were counted among the 120,000 immigrants the government boasts of having brought to the country during the last year, at a cost of $560,000. The government will take credit to themselves for bringing these 2,000 people out. It was said by the Minister of the Interior that the Barr colonists were every one satisfied. Where are they to-day ? Are they on their colony ? If they were satisfied in every particular, would you not expect to find them there ? They left England to go there. They believed that was to be their future home, where they would live for the^ remainder of their days ; but some of them did not survey the promised land from Pisgnh's top. Where are they to-day? Some of them. I am told, folded up their tents in the night, like the Egyptians, and left the country. You will find many of

Before you leave the Chair, Sir, I wish to draw the attention of the government to an item which appeared in the speech from the Throne :
The great influx of population into our Northwestern territories and the very large additional areas of fertile land which are being brought under cultivation combine to further press upon us the need for increased transportation facilities for the forwarding of our grain and other products to the markets of the world, through Canadian channels. The whole question of transportation and terminal facilities continues to occupy much attention, and my government will immediately appoint a commission of experienced men to report on the subject.

It is about eighteen weeks ago since that statement was put in the mouth of His Excellency by the government, and notwithstanding the reports throughout the country that ail arrangement has been made with certain parties for the purpose of building railways into the North-west Territories and tlie statement by the right lion, the First Minister that a commission had been appointed to look into the question of transportation facilities, this House has not vet been informed as to the policy of the government with reference to the first matter and as to the personnel of the commission to inquire into transportation facilities. The organs supporting the government have published what they say is the policy of the government on the question of building railways into the North-west. On reading that publication, I expected that the government would in a day or two have announced its policy, and I would ask whether the hon. gentleman who is now leading the House is prepared to state what that policy is ? If he is not prepared to do so, when may we expect a declaration on behalf of the government, as it is certainly high time they took the country into their confidence ?

No objection whatever can be taken to the inquiry of my hon. friend with regard to the very important questions to which he has referred. Unfortunately, there has been a difficulty in obtaining commissioners such as the country would desire. The position of commissioner was offered to a gentleman of great experience, and for a considerable length of time he was unable to give an answer. It was deemed so important that his services, if possible, should be secured, that no other arrangement was made to secure some one in his place, the hope being entertained that sooner or later he would be able to accept the office. Within a very short time he has written to the minister expressing liis doubt as to tbo ability to procood at piesent, and has put us in the position of either having to make another appointment or wait a little longer to see if he will accept. I am sure that the hon. gentleman would be the last one to wish that the couu-try should lose, if it is at all possible to secure them, the services of Sir William Van Horne in this matter. I have not had, within the last few days, any conversation with my hon. colleague the Minister of Public Works, but will bring the matter to his attention, and perhaps on Monday we will be able to speak more definitely 'regarding the choice of commissioners.

speechtext: This opposition have not criticised fully many of the estimates that have gone through. speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Why is it in committee at this late date ? Our leader was ready to meet hon. gentlemen opposite at any time. But no committee was appointed for a long time, and when it was appointed how soon was it called together ? The delay is not due to the leader of the opposition or to gentlemen associated witli him, hut it is due to the dilatoriness of hon. gentlemen opposite. It has been the same with every measure in the hands of the ministers. Though we have been here four months, they are coming down day after day with important measures that ought to have been introduced at the opening of the session. It is practically cruelty to animals to keep members in this chamber at this date with no ventilation. I hope the ministers will have a consultation among themselves, and see if something cannot be done to improve the ventilation of this chamber. The engineer tells the Minister of Public Works that if these windows are opened the fans are no good. There are a couple of fans in No. 10, and they have the effect of keeping lion, gentlemen opposite cool. But here in the chamber we have no ventilation and in No. 0 we have no fans to keep us cool. We are in a sweat-box here. But we can stand the sweat-box as long as hon. gentlemen opposite can. Why, the ministers will not come into this chamber themselves. One or two of them told me that they would not come in to-night.
It is made too hot for them.

By that time, they might agree among themselves what measure they will bung down and push through. They can put through any measure they please because they have a following behind them that is strong enough to enable them to have their own way. This faithful opposition is doing its duty in criticising rascalities and extravagances of this government. But we do not offer criticism that the acts of the government would fully justify. I draw the attention of the minister to the fact that no policy lias yet been settled upon in reference to the sales of the islands lying south of Moose Deer Point on the Georgian bay. There are hundreds of islands there and they are anxiously sought for by Canadians and Americans who desire to build summer residences. It is admitted that the islands north of Moose Deer Point are under the control of the Ontario government, but the title to those south of that point has been in dispute. I would like to ask the minister whether any arrangement has been come to with the province of Ontario as to the ownership of these islands. If such an arrangement has been arrived at I would impress upon the minister that at a very early date he should sell these islands, and that the sale should be by public auction

and not by private tender. If the sale were conducted at Midland or Penetanguishene, to which places there are excellent railway facilities, very considerable prices could be secured at public auction.

Shortly after I took office I caused a survey to be made of these islands. I was proceeding to take the necessary steps to have them sold when the Ontario government protested on the ground that the islands south of Moose Deer point belonged to them. We are fairly well satisfied that they belong to the Indian Department in trust for the Indians, but that can only be settled by an appeal to the courts. I have discussed the question a number of times with the representatives of Ontario, but as there are a great many questions unsettled between that province and the Dominion it is difficult to get any one question re-, ferred for settlement without all the rest. Two years ago I had the whole subject of dispute carefully investigated by two very capable officers of the department who made a confidential report. I am desirous of having these questions in dispute referred to a joint commission. The Ontario government do not oppose any serious objection to a joint commission, but we have not as yet been able to come to an agreement. I appreciate what my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) said, that whereas some years ago there was no large demand for these islands it may now be desirable that they should be placed upon the market. I hope to have these matters in dispute settled as soon ns possible.

I think perhaps the province of Ontario and this government could come to an arrangement by which the islands might be sold and the proceeds credited to the Indian fund, and if it were afterwards held that the province of Ontario was entitled to the money it could be recouped. Campers now go on these islands and fires spread, and the islands are rapidly deteriorating from the aesthetic point of view which makes them less desirable for summer residences. If any sale does take place I impress upon the minister to have it by public auction and not by tender.

I am indisposed to think that an arrangement could be made for the sale of the islands and the money afterwards applied as may be decided upon by competent authority. I have not pressed an arrangement of that kind because, although occasionally we do have inquiries, there was nothing before me that indicated any special demands for these islands. I note what the hon. gentleman says about selling them by auction. I may say that the experience of the department has not been altogether to the effect that sales by auction were more satisfactory than sales by tender, but I will | give the suggestion of the hon. member'
(Mr. Bennett) due consideration before anything is done.

I hope an arrangement may be come to soon because if a sale is held by auction during the coming fall I think considerable purchases would be made and the purchasers could go on with the erection of their residences in the winter or early spring. May I ask the minister what islands if any have been disposed of during the past year, below Moose Deer point ?

At this moment I cannot say exactly. My hon. friend will remember that an application was made for two islands, which were sold. To the best of my recollection some two or three others were sold, and they were sold after we had received letters from the Crown Lands Department of the province of Ontario, saying that there was no objection to the sale, we agreeing on our part to hold the money until it should be decided later how it should be disposed of.

I would like to bring to the notice of the minister a case that occurred in my own constituency. A small island in Pigeon lake was sold by Mr. Boyd, a wealthy man, to a poor man, who paid for the island and went on it and built n house. Some time afterwards Mr. Boyd found that he did not own the island, and paid the money baek. The man was very desirous of getting a title to the island, and referred the matter to the department here ; but the department replied that no title could be given to him because the island belonged to the Indians. In view of the fact that these islands, according to this discussion, can be disposed of, I do not see why this poor man cannot get a remedy.

The island referred to by the hon. gentleman consists of Indian lands that have not been surrendered. The department has no authority to sell any islands that have not been surrendered by the Indian band. After the surrender is executed we hold the land in trust and sell it. The only thing we could do would be to apply to the baud for a surrender of that particular island. Whenever it is surrendered, the department will endeavour to protect the right of this man, and see that no one else gets it.
It will be a great satisfaction to this man if he receives that information from the department.
I am told by the deputy that that is the position the department has taken.

I wish to call the minister's attention to a matter that came to my notice recently in connection with the Walpole island band. The case is shortly this :	A man named Johnston, some ten
years ago adopted a young Indian boy seven

years of age. Tlie father of the boy was then dead ; his mother is still a widow. The child was adopted, not under any writing, hut by an agreement with the mother. The boy's name is Sand. He was kept until last April or May, between nine and ten years, when he was turned out. Even a portion of his clothing was retained by this man Johnston or his wife. During that whole period the child has been sent little or no time to school, and has been kept all the time at work. He is now sixteen years of age, and has been turned adrift without either schooling or any other provision being made for him. Johnston also drew the boy's annuity during the period he was with him, which, so far as I can find out, was about $3.50 a year. X took some pains to question the mother as to whether she had ever assented to this. She said she had never assented to it, that Johnston had managed, by giving the child as one of his own household, to receive the annuity. I made further inquiry as to whether the boy had disobeyed or whether there had been some quarrel or difference to cause the boy to be turned out. The mother informed me that the boy had gone to a tea meeting, and when he returned home, he found the door locked against him, they would not let him in, and he remained out all night. She tells me that an application was made to the department to have an inquiry, and that the agent, Mr. McDougail, had informed her that there would be no inquiry into the matter. He accepted the statement of Johnston, who is the wealthiest Indian on the island, who has acquired a good deal of property, and is quite responsible in that way. If the facts are as I have stated, it is certainly a very aggravated case. The boy's mother informs me that if there is an investigation, she is prepared to make these statements good. I would suggest that the investigation be held by some other person than the Indian agent. I do not care to give my reasons for saying that, nor do I want it understood that it implies any reflection.

The ordinary course in such a case would be for the inspector to be instructed to investigate and report upon his first visit to the reserve. If I understand my hon. friend aright, the matter was referred to the agent, and he declined to do anything. We will write to the agent and obtain a statement of the facts, and, if on that statement nothing can be done, we will have the inspector look into the case on his first visit to the reserve. The hon. gentleman will see that it is pretty difficult to tell the Indian to take this boy back unless he is willing to do it. The grievance is obvious but the remedy is not quite so obvious. Possibly, with the influence of the inspector, something may be done.

Is it not possible that this man, who failed to carry out the agreement,
could be compelled to make some restitution ? It may be difficult to make him take the boy back.

Such a contract would have no legal validity. But the circumstances may justify the department in withholding this man's annuity, if he be entitled to one, until we secure the amount he collected in the shape of the boy's annuity, so that a refund would be secured.

There might be some doubt about the validity of the contract, but in cases of that kind arising outside of Indians it is obviously clear that where a child is kept and it is proved that there was even a verbal arrangement, and also proved that the child was deprived of schooling, there would be not only an equitable but possibly a legal claim against the person who adopted the child.
Between white people, such a verbal arrangement would have no legal effect. The agreement would have to be embodied in a formal legal instrument, properly executed.

Will the hon. gentleman have the matter investigated right away ? There has already been correspondence with the department, and I think that the correspondence has been principally the agent's view of the case. I do not care to say more than I have said, but I think that an investigation ought to take place before some one other than the agent.
My deputy tells me that the inspector looked into the matter a short time ago. I will have the correspondence 'brought before me and give instructions to the inspector to investigate and report.

The history of the Indian fund is very complicated. Some years ago it was thought that the expenditure had impaired some of the funds, which were trust funds held for certain services. One of the funds impaired was the Indian Land Management Fund. The result of the inquiry some years ago showed the total amount by which the fund has been impaired, and an Order in Council was passed 'by the late government providing that an annual payment of $14,000 should be voted for a number of years for the purpose of recouping the fund and putting it back into the position into which it was and ought to be. When the plan of gradual restitution of this fund was put into operation, the capital was as follows.

So that the fund has increased during the ten years by $104,000.
This fund, the Indian land management fund, would be restored in about twenty years, by an annual payment of about $14,000, to the position in which it originally stood. Hon. gentlemen understand that the fund originally arose from percentages on the sales of Indian property. It came into the hands of the government as a trust fund. But, through non-observance of the rule that only the interest should be expended, the department impaired the fund.
To provide lor the erection ol lockup at St. Regis, $500.
I see that a similar amount to this was voted last year.

Yes, but we did not build the lock-up. We have had a good deal of difficulty on this reserve, as the hon. gentleman knows. Two years ago the difficulty became quite serious. The St. Regis Indians are of a somewhat turbulent character, and they give the department a good deal of trouble. A little over a year ago, some of the Indians undertook to take possession of islands in the St. Lawrence which had been leased a long time ago, it is true, but on investigation I found that the leases were sound, and the parties had gone' into possession-and we had to take legal proceedings and notified them that if they went any further we would proceed against them very seriously. Our officer said that we ought to have a lock-up on the reserve and some changes in the administration. I am going about the changes slowly. The state of feeling now is much better, and I shall probably carry out my intention with regard to the lock-up this year. I did not think it prudent to do so last year. If the lock-up had been built Hon. Mr. SIFTON.
so soon after the other proceedings, the exasperation of these people might have led to some trouble. Having asserted the law, so far as the islands were concerned, I thought I had done enough and had better let the lock-up stand until this year.
Was there no lock-up there before ?

No ; it was talked about, but never built.
General legal expenses, $3,500.
We would like some explanation as to this.

This is to cover the expense of defending Indians when they are accused of criminal offences. In all very serious cases, where we have to employ counsel, this is done through the Justice Department, and, of course, we have to pay.
To whom were the amounts paid last year ?
About $1,000 was paid, mainly in the defence of an Indian tried in Hull.
What legal firm was it paid to ?
1 have not the name at hand, but I will get it a little later.

May I ask for information with regard to items in the Auditor General's Report, at page J-163, moneys paid to E. Stewart, forestry inspector. Do I understand that Mr. E. Stewart is in the hon. minister's department ?
It must be the same man-yes.
Is he paid a stated salary ?

Yes ; by the Interior Department-not by the Indian Department. I am told by the officers of the department that Mr. Stewart was instructed to make certain valuations for the Indian Department, being the officer most capable for doing it that we had available at the time, and this money was paid for expenses.
- Mr. BLAIN. These payments include : Valuing White Fish river reserve, $70.55 ; valuing White Fish island, $69.35.

I am assured by the officers of the department that Mr. Stewart received nothing but travelling expenses. Of course, as Mr. Stewart is in the civil service and receives a regular salary-he is paid $2,500 a year- it would be illegal for any branch of the government to pay him anything further as salary or fees. So the hon. gentleman will see that it is quite impossible that he should have been paid anything except his expenses.

Tliis gentleman Is receiving a very large salary In tlie lion, minister's department. The hon. minister tells us that the payment to which I have just called attention is for travelling expenses. It does not so appear in the Auditor General's Report. Would the hon. minister tell us where, in the Auditor General's Report, a detailed statement of these expenses is to be found 7 This gentleman is receiving a very large salary of $2,500

The amount of his salary had nothing to do with his expenses. He gets a salary for liis entire time. The Indian Department, requiring certain reserves to be valued, I presume got authority that Hr. Stewart should be directed to do the work. Of course, he could not charge his expenses to the Interior Department, for they had nothing to do with it. We practically took his time from the Interior Department, got him to do the work and paid his expenses. The hon. gentleman will see that there is more than one item :
E. Stewart, forestry inspector, Interior Department, travelling expenses : arbitration Gros Cap reserve, $84.60 ; valuing White Pish River reserve, $70.55 ; valuing White Fish Island, $69.35, $224.50.
These are three distinct services.
Nova Scotia-relief and seed grain for Indians, $2,700.
Is that item put in every year because you are sure you will need it, or only because you want to have it available ?

The amount expended in 1901-2 was $2,699. A large proportion of the Indians have to be given some small supply, which is however cut down to the lowest possible notch. Those who have land ready for cultivation are given a small quantity of seed.
Why is the minister asking for $3,500 for legal expenses, when the amount expended last year was only $1,000 ? Does he anticipate some further trouble ?

The vote for legal expenses is merely a general estimate. When we have three or four cases in the course of a year, we have to pay the expenses out of something, and if we'do not have this vote we will not have the money. This is a maximum estimate. If we do not need the money we do not expend it. The amount is arrived at by the experience of the department in past years.
How much has been expended each year for the last four or five years ?

I have no way of getting at the exact amounts. The reason we ask for this vote
is because last year the department was embarrassed in finding itself liable to pay these amounts, and being obliged to hold over the accounts until a vote could be obtained. I always take a vote every year for $1,000; sometimes we do not use it, and sometimes we spend it all. It is a vote for protection purposes for the defence of the Indians. That is done under the Department of Justice, who employ counsel, and decide whether it is a proper case in which to employ counsel. That department taxes the bill of costs, certifies to the correctness of the amount and it is paid.
I understood the minister to say that there was only one case last year. Would he give us the particulars of that case ?
The case was that of an Indian tried at Hull for murder. I am told that the Bill of the lawyers employed was taxed in the usual way by the Department of Justice.

How much was the amount of the bill ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
About $1,000. The current year's account does not appear in the Auditor General's Report yet.

Does that include the witnesses fees and everything else ?
The	MINISTER	OP	THE	INTERIOR.
All the expenses were about $1,000.

How much of that would be for solicitors' fees and how much for the other disbursements ?
The	MINISTER	OP	THE	INTERIOR.
I have not got the figures here. But if the hon. gentleman desires to have that information I will get it.
I would like to see that.

This is the case of an Indian named Waby who killed one McCabe up near the headwaters of the Ottawa river.	The	Indian .was
brought down here to Hull to be tried, and while he was here, the court-house was burned, and he was removed to Montreal, but brought back again to be tried. A great number of the witnesses had to be brought from the upper waters of the Ottawa river, which necessitated a large expenditure. This case was one that attracted a good deal of attention, Mr. McCabe being a man of some importance in the district in connection with the fur trading business, and the case was a -hard fought case. The crown was under obligation to defend this man. The expense was somewhat large by reason of the fact that in the province of Quebec they had a mixed jury, that is to say, one-lialf English and one-half French. We had to have two counsel also, one French and one English, and an interpreter. These costs were all fixed in the regular way. I

think the gentlemen who defended this prisoner were allowed $25 a day during the course of the trial. The hill was taxed according to the practice that has prevailed in the Department of Justice for many years, and I am safe in saying that all the taxation that has been done-I do not claim any credit for it myself, because that is something I never interfere with-it is done by the officials of the department, and the hoii. gentleman will see by referring to the bill that nothing was allowed except that to which the counsel are honestly entitled. The whole taxation was done by Mr. Gisborne, and done with the greatest possible care.
Did I understand that the counsel were only allowed $25 each ?
Each of them $25 a day.
How much was the total disbursement altogether for counsel and witness fees ?
My hou. friend will admit that it is absolutely impossible to bear in mind the details of an account of that description. This occurred at least a year and a half ago.
I assume the hon. minister has the figures showing what it cost up to date.
The Bill comes to us in detail, it is taxed in the Department of Justice and then sent back for payment to the Indian Department. The Bill can be produced here.
We will give the exact details if the hon. gentleman desires it.
Who are the counsel ?
Mr. Devlin, of Hull, was one, and Mr. Decarie, of Montreal, was another.
Could Mr-. Devlin not speak both English and French ?

I think there are about three or four counsel in Quebec who will undertake to conduct trials in English and French.
Mr. BwVIN. How much was voted for this service last year ?
The same amount.
The hon. minister should be able to give us the information as to how much has been expended on legal services by the department during the last five years.
I could not give it to the hon. gentleman, but I will have the information looked up.
Last year there was an exceptional trial and the item was about

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: $1,000. I am not complaining about that, but I think it is only fair to the committee, when the hon. gentleman is asking for a vote of $3,500 and when last year there was only $1,000 expended and that an exceptional expenditure, that the hon. gentleman should give us some further explanation. In only one year during the last six years has $1,000 been expended. There is a general complaint that outside of this department large expenses are paid for legal services. It seems to me that it would be better to vote only double the amount expended last year rather than to vote $3,500.

The amount voted does not make the least difference in the amount that the department has to pay. Cases come before me constantly and the Department of Justice has to decide in each of these whether it is a proper case to defend or not. If it is a proper case for the department to defend, the determination to defend it is not based on the fact as to whether we have a vote or as to whether we have not. After it is decided to defend the case the Department of Justice designates the lawyer to take charge of it and the next step is that the Department of Justice certifies the Bill and sends it to us to pay. If we have not sufficient money to pay it we would have to ask for a supplementary vote. This is a mere estimate on the part of the officers of the department, and they have estimated it at what they believe to be a perfectly safe amount. If circumstances require us to pay this amount we will pay it, and if they do not of course the vote will lapse.
Mi'. BLAIN. It is not a usual practice to vote nearly three times as much as the average yearly expenditure has been. If hon. gentlemen did that in every department the estimates would be three times as much.
The vote might be $100 and we might only pay out $5.

I understand that. The hon. minister might as well say that his department needs $1,000 because the expenditure has been $1,000. Yet, he comes down and asks for a vote of $3,500. Surely it has not been customary to pursue a policy of that kind. I admit this item is not a very large one, but it seems to me that some little mischief might creep into the department as a result of a vote of this kind.
I wish to ask some questions about the item of ' relief and seed grain, $2,700.' I did not hear that item called.
It was called several times.

1 am sure the hou. Minister of the Interior will give the information.
The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR Last year we expended $2,099 and we are asking for practically the same amount this year. This expenditure was for relief, providing the actual necessaries of life, si me seed grain and a small amount has been paid out during the last two years for fertilizers.

Does it not seem a little strange that you should include fertilizers in the item for relief, and seed grain ?
Medical attendance and medicines, $3,700.
I understand that this is a new item. Would the hon. minister tell us if they have a regular medical man, and if so, how much the department pay him ?

Do you pay them by the visit or by the year ?
We pay them by the year in each case. The officers of the department have based the amount upon the accounts which were rendered in former years.
If there should be an epidemic of small-pox on a reserve would the medical officer only get his salary of $300 a year.

He gets the same salary right along. I have
in one or two cases allowed a certain amount extra to be paid when an epidemic of small-pox broke out.
Does this salary include the supply of medicine as well.

Yes.
Indians, Manitoba, North-west Territories, $841,921.

I will make a general statement as to this vote. As to the annuities, they are payable to the Indians under treaty, and the amount only varies by the number of Indians. There is a vote for $7,949 for agricultural implements which is $4,000 less than last year. Each Indian agent makes up a detailed bill showing every particular item which lie requires, and sends it to the commissioner at Winnipeg, who sends it down here.
How are all these supplies purchased ?

The purchases generally in the Indian Department are made by tender. We have printed schedules and we advertise it once a year, and let the contract. There are some few things that are purchased from dealers in the vicinity of the reserve, it is cheaper to pay the retail price there than to buy them here and ship them up. We ask a vote of $20,295 for live stock for the Indians. This vote is a little less than last year. I have increased that vote since I came to office considerably in pursuance of the policy of inducing what we regard as the more troublesome Indians to go into stock raising. The last report of the Indian Department shows that the results are very encouraging. We send pedigreed stock to the reserve, and my information is that about the best grade stock that can be found in the North-west Territories is to be found upon some of the Indian reserves as a result of the policy which was inaugurated by the late government and which I have extended as the late government intended to extend it if it was found to be successful. The Indians in the Calgary district, the Bloods, Piegans and Blackfeet, the most dangerous and difficult Indians to manage, have been induced to go into the cattle raising to a very considerable extent, and I think that in five or six years perhaps we shall be able to discontinue the practice of giving rations altogether as a result of the policy we are following in this respect.
How do you purchase this $20,000 worth of live stock?
We simply purchase from different breeders and dealers and pay the current price. The cattle have to pass inspection.
How is the allotment made-per capita or according to the wants of the particular tribe ?

It is a sort of paternal arrangement. The difficulty in past years on a considerable number of the reserves has been to get the Indians to take the cattle on any terms and agree to look after them. As my hon. friend has said, they probably kill them and eat them in a short time. . We have been giving them cattle as fast as they manifest a disposition to look after them and take proper care of them. Some Indians go into wheat raising and others into cattle raising, and we endeavour to consult their habits in carrying out the policy of the department.
I find on page J-15 of the Auditor General's Report that three of the largest amounts expended for live stock were on the Blackfoot, Blood and Piegan reserves. Are they all south of Calgary ?
They are all in the neighbourhood of Calgary.

How is it that the grants for these three tribes were so large as compared with the others ? Two of them run to nearly $4,000 each, and the others to about $3,000.
The MINISTER OF THEi INTERIOR. It is only lately that we have been able to do anything with these reserves. They are large bands of Indians. I would like my hon. friend to look into the report in regard to them.

I happened to be at Macleod last fall and I saw a number of these Indians in the town. They were selling hay. They certainly presented a much more civilized appearance than most of the Indians one sees in the west. From what I heard, they have a very desirable reserve for raising cattle; and It seemed odd that though cattle raising is being carried on more extensively in the neighbourhood of Macleod than in'any other part of the country they should be so far behind. They were Bloods and I think Blaekfeet. It seems odd that they should require such a very large expenditure, as compared with other reserves.

It is only within the last few years that these Indians have been willing to take the cattle upon condition of looking after them. They are not yet iby any means making use of all the grazing privileges on their reserves. For instance, it is only lately that we have made arrangements with regard to the Piegan reserve, on condition of the Indians leasing a portion of the reserve for grazing purposes.
Where are the Piegans?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: Nine miles south-west of Macleod.
What do you do with the Indians who kill their cattle and eat them ? Do you punish them in any way ?

That is a matter of individual discretion on the part of the agent. You cannot apply any hard and fast rule. We believe it would not be wise to incur any disaffection on the part of the Blood Indians on that account; and the agent, in dealing with the matter, requires to bring to bear his knowledge of the Indian character and to take into account the circumstances of the case.
Did you supply the Sar-cee Indians with any cattle last year ?
No, they refused to take them.
I noticed one cow on the reserve, seven or eight miles west of Calgary; and if they took care of all their reserve stock as they did that cow, I do not believe it would be prudent to supply them.
Are the supplies of tea and other groceries Which are distributed among the different tribes, bought by tender and public competition ?
Yes. The supplies generally are advertised at the head office of the department under schedules. .
I ask that question because I see that political friends of the government in Ottawa and Toronto alone seem to furnish the supplies.

I must say that the political friends of the government do not profit very much from the Indian supplies, because I do not think the prices could be cut any closer than they are. The schedules are known to the trade all over the country, and the competition is very close.
Might I ask how the agricultural implements are purchased ? Is it by tender ?

Most of them are purchased on the ground from agents. The number of implements purchased is comparatively small, so that it is very difficult to buy them in bulk. The prices are practically the same to all parties, because agricultural implements are sold on schedule prices.
I see that $20,000 in round figures was paid for beef on the Blood agency last year. Were tenders called for that ?

Yes, that is all purchased by tender. This vote represents the general supplies we are

required to furnish the Indians, when they are paid their treaty money under the treaties on the various reserves. There are large quantities of bacon, beef, tea, flour, tobacco, ammunition and twine and a small quantity of medicine. Large quantities are purchased by tenders. The increase to the vote for schools is due to increased attendance. The vote for surveys is due to the fact that occasionally we have an Indian reserve surrendered, and we have to survey it and advertise it for sale by public tender. The increase in general expenses is due to a number of small items, and to some increases in salaries.
No, but we had to purchase an engine for the grist-mill, Crooked Lake Reserve, as the old one was condemned by the government inspector.

Has it always been the custom to supply building materials to the Indians ? I see some correspondence with the Auditor General on that point.
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
Not generally.

Is this a new item entirely?'
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
It is not customary to furnish building material for the Indians' houses. I presume this is for the work in connection with the agency buildings.

As to the inspector of Indian agencies, I see an estimate here for the salary of J. A. Macrae. I thought we were told that when Mr. Wadsworth was allowed to go, we were to do without an inspector of Indian agencies.

This is only an inspector for the province of Ontario. Mr. Wadsworth was inspector for the North-west Territories, Mr. Macrae who has been in office for a great many years, was formerly in the North-west Territories, but was brought down here. He is one of the inspectors for the older provinces, and rngkes inspections from time to time, pays annuity money, and so on.

But I understood that when Mr. Wadsworth was allowed to go the hon. minister said that he would do away with that office. I am told that since then, instead of the office being done away with, there are two men doing the work that Mr. Wadsworth did, and that they are not' only paid salaries, but get amounts from other branches as well.
The MINISTER ' OF THE INTERIOR. Mr. Wadsworth was superannuated in connection with the general rearrangement of the work. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) is misinformed if he has been told that two men are doing the work this officer used to do. It is quite the other way-only part of one man's time is devoted to that work.
I have personal knowledge of the facts, and can speak of the efficiency of the service.
I would like to have this item stand, and the hon. gentleman bring me the information with regard to it.

THE HOUSE.	*
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved the adjournment of the House.

Before the House adjourns, I would ask the hon. minister who is leading the House at present if he would be good enough to tell us when the government hope to make its statement to the House regarding its railway policy. We see a good deal about it in the press. It seems to me it is baldly dealing fairly with the House if the government is not prepared to lay its policy before the House, that it should give it to the country through its own press. I think the hon. gentleman should be able to tell us that now. There must be some conclusion reached.

As an old journalist, I would advise my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) not to place too much reliance upon statements in the press as regards matters of this kind. At present we are not in a position to say anything to the House, but if there was anything to say, I would anticipate that the Prime Minister would make a statement next week.
What business may we expect to take up next Monday ?
There are several Bills and resolutions on the Order Paper to be dealt with, and, if we reach supply, we will go on with the estimates of the Minister of the Interior.
